]]>danindub<![CDATA[Irish firms lag behind global peers in managing cyber risk, PwC finds]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/19/irish-firms-lag-behind-global-peers-in-managing-cyber-risk-pwc-finds/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/19/irish-firms-lag-behind-global-peers-in-managing-cyber-risk-pwc-finds/Mon, 19 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000Irish companies lag behind their global counterparts in integrating cybersecurity into their risk management, new research by PwC has found.

A survey of 4,000 business and tech executives from 71 countries, including Ireland, found 17 per cent of Irish respondents strongly agreed that cybersecurity was fully part of their organisation’s overall risk management, compared to 41 per cent globally.

PwC Ireland cybersecurity and privacy partner Leonard McAuliffe said that as many organisations are racing to capture the value of AI, preparation for cyber risks “needs to become a business capability”.

“The survey finds many organisations are still underprepared for a rapidly evolving cyber landscape, and organisations that get this right will be better positioned to innovate with confidence while continuing to operate through disruption,” McAuliffe said.

The results of the survey also showed only 23 per cent of Irish respondents strongly agreed their employer regularly conducted incident response exercises, compared with 41 per cent globally.

Against a backdrop of rapid advances in AI, 84 per cent of global security and finance leaders said they expect their cyber budgets to rise over the next 12 months.

Responses from Irish participants also indicated protection against AI-enabled attacks was a lower spending priority, as 34 per cent identified securing against AI-enabled attacks as a cyber spending priority compared with 46 per cent globally.

Irish executives showed they are wary of adopting autonomous AI tools as part of their cyber defence. Only 6 per cent said they would allow AI agents to act fully autonomously to help protect their systems versus 22 per cent globally.

How HR teams are combatting AI and other security threats in recruitment process

On a global basis, 29 per cent of companies said quantum-computing exposure was a cyber threat that their organisation is least prepared to combat in the next 12 months, and Ireland lags behind global counterparts.

Quantum computing is expected to break current encryption protocols as early as the 2030s, according to the PwC report, and only 6 per cent of Irish respondents said that they are implementing quantum-resistant security measures compared to 21 per cent globally.

]]>NurPhoto<![CDATA[Hotel planned on central Dublin site after investor rules offices and housing ‘not viable’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/19/hotel-planned-on-central-dublin-site-after-investor-rules-offices-and-housing-not-viable/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/19/hotel-planned-on-central-dublin-site-after-investor-rules-offices-and-housing-not-viable/Mon, 19 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000German property investor KGAL plans to replace a Dublin city-centre office block with a hotel after concluding that neither extending the office nor redeveloping the site for housing would be financially viable.

The investor’s proposal adds to signs of a shift from office development in Dublin, with Core Capital’s Derek McGrath and Johnny Ronan’s development group also pivoting towards hotel construction.

Earlier this month, KGAL’s Irish subsidiary Golden Lane Liffey Limited sought permission from Dublin City Council to demolish 31-36 Golden Lane and build a new midmarket 225-room hotel beside the Radisson Blu Royal Hotel near South Great George’s Street.

The property was extensively refurbished after being let to San Francisco tech firm New Relic on a 20-year lease in 2017, but has been vacant since the company moved out last year.

KGAL said in its application that several options were explored for the site, which included extending the existing three-storey office from 2,800sq m to 6,700sq m across eight storeys and refurbishing the block into 59 apartments or 160 student beds.

Aviva seeks operator for new luxury hotel on Dublin’s Clarendon Street

It added that demolition of the building and construction of a new hotel was the only viable financial option.

“Given the current high level of office vacancy rates, the emergence of the ‘work from home’ model and the site’s location outside of the core office districts, the redevelopment of the subject site for office use is not financially viable,” KGAL’s planning application said.

Feasibility studies added that a financially viable apartment block would be difficult to build because the site’s “constrained nature” meant it would be difficult to meet residential development standards. Similar constraints “render it not possible” for student accommodation of sufficient scale to be viable.

A letter attached to the submission from student accommodation investor Urbanest said the site would need to house at least 200 bed spaces to be viable to run on a cost-per-bed space ratio.

KGAL’s application added that there had been strong demand for further hotel accommodation in Dublin based on occupancy across seven competing hotels exceeding 90 per cent in the summer of 2026.

Tenant exit and flat rents weigh on €300m Dublin office portfolio

The new hotel proposal has come soon after Ronan Group sought approval to change its redevelopment plans for the current Citigroup building in Dublin’s International Financial Services Centre and replace 40 per cent of planned office space with two new hotels.

McGrath’s Renmark Property Holdings Limited also plans to change its development plans for a site near the RDS in Ballsbridge, where it has permission for an eight-storey office block.

Last week, McGrath told the Business Post his firm had decided to develop a 244-bedroom hotel and a 194-bedroom aparthotel on the site instead due to uncertainty in the office market.

KGAL, which manages €15 billion of assets globally, acquired 31-36 Golden Lane for €25.5 million in 2018 from Peter Leonard and Derek Pippinga’s Mm Capital. The latest accounts for Golden Lane Liffey Limited valued the property at €20.1 million.

The building was pre-let to tech firm New Relic on a €1.4-million-a-year, 20-year lease deal in 2017 and then went through an extensive refurbishment before the company moved in a year later.

New Relic, which indicated it would grow its Irish headcount from 100 to 300 following the move to Golden Lane, has cut back its Irish office from 117 to 90 staff since 2022 and relocated to new offices on Pearse Street in 2025.

]]><![CDATA[CarVal generates €310m surplus in four years from loan portfolios bought for €1bn]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/19/carval-generates-310m-surplus-in-four-years-from-loan-portfolios-bought-for-1bn/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/19/carval-generates-310m-surplus-in-four-years-from-loan-portfolios-bought-for-1bn/Mon, 19 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000Loan investment vehicles linked to US debt group AB CarVal Investors have generated a gross surplus of €310 million from collections and the resale of Irish property loans they acquired for €1.02 billion since 2022.

In 2022, AB CarVal’s Irish vehicle Braunton Property Finance Designated Activity Company (DAC) bought a portfolio of Irish residential mortgages from KBC Bank Ireland and Premier Homeloans for €610.2 million.

The Minneapolis-based firm’s subsidiary Hartland Property Finance then paid Bank of Ireland €410.4 million in 2023 for a separate portfolio of distressed Irish residential and commercial property loans.

New financial filings by AB CarVal’s firms, which cover the 2025 financial year, show Braunton will be wound up after it “sold its remaining portfolio of loans”, and Hartland has also sold a large portion of the debt it acquired in 2023.

An analysis by The Irish Times of financial statements for Braunton has shown it made €764.9 million from both the collection and resale of the KBC Bank Ireland and Premier Homeloans it acquired for €610.2 million – a surplus of €154.7 million.

Hartland has recorded a surplus of €155.3 million after making €565.7 million from both the collection and resale of loans linked to the portfolio it bought from Bank of Ireland for €410.4 million. The €565.7 million total for Hartland includes €90.8 million of proceeds it made from a sale of part of its portfolio in April 2026.

The combined €310 million surplus represents proceeds above the original purchase costs before financing costs, operating expenses and tax expenses.

The disclosures follow reporting by The Irish Times earlier this year that showed AB CarVal’s Elmscott Property Finance also made a €75 million profit in the space of three years from flipping some non-performing personal and commercial debt, valued at €694 million, that it bought from Ulster Bank in August 2023 for €268 million.

Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings have shown a special-purpose entity linked to the investment bank Goldman Sachs called Penryn Funding 2024 DAC acquired some of the debt sold by AB CarVal’s vehicles, Hartland and Elmscott.

Minneapolis-based AB CarVal was one of the first foreign funds to move on Ireland after the financial crash, and among the most prolific purchasers of distressed Irish debt.

The firm bought non-performing loans valued at billions of euro, including loans connected to the Irish Banking Resolution Corporation’s (IBRC) Project Stone loan portfolio, which was valued at a combined €6.85 billion, and a collection of 5,000 loans called Project Poseidon that included assets such as the Lyrath Estate Hotel in Kilkenny and the Regency Hotel in Dublin.

Following the recovery of the Irish economy, AB CarVal has continued to use its office in Ireland as a hub to manage distressed debt in other parts of Europe.

]]><![CDATA[Why London looks better than ever for a business shindig]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/19/why-london-looks-better-than-ever-for-a-business-shindig/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/19/why-london-looks-better-than-ever-for-a-business-shindig/Mon, 19 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000As deadly Houthi missiles smashed into Riyadh’s international airport last week, people from around the world still made their way to the Saudi capital for one of the biggest oil and gas industry conferences on the calendar.

When they arrived at the WPC Energy Congress, in some cases having driven for hours to avoid flying, they found a number of prominent names on the agenda had gone missing. The bosses of ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies, Shell and BP had pulled out after the attacks, which killed at least a dozen people and injured hundreds more.

I expect more big names will skip another international conference due to start in a week in Riyadh – the so-called Davos in the Desert.

This probably won’t be the last time this happens in a complicated world showing no sign of improvement. A string of Middle East trade shows and conventions has already been cancelled or deferred as the Iran war grinds on. The street arrests and travel restrictions by Donald Trump’s administration continue to drive international academic conferences away from the US to other countries.

As a frequent conference-goer myself, these dispiriting sights have made me wonder: which cities are now deemed the best places for business gatherings?

To my surprise, it turns out I am living in one of them.

London was named the best city in Europe for events and meetings this year for the fourth year in a row in a closely watched ranking by the Cvent conference tech group.

Yet again we beat Barcelona, Madrid and Lisbon. Even Paris only managed fifth place.

I say “we”, even though I am a transplanted Australian, one of the more than 40 per cent of Londoners who are foreign-born. As it happens, that is a higher share than you will find in Paris, Berlin and even New York City – a pleasing reminder that London is one of the most diverse major cities on the planet.

Take the Tube that we all moan about constantly, and is admittedly expensive, but still zips you across the city in a sliver of the time it takes to cover such distances in other big cities

Cvent makes scant mention of this in its list of reasons for ranking London so highly. But the factors it does cite underscore how revealing it is to look at your city as an outsider.

The sprawling conference centres I am occasionally required to trek out to for work are apparently world-class.

London Southend Airport, which I have never technically been to, means we have six airports. There are also more than 80 Michelin-starred restaurants and, by Cvent’s count, 200 museums, 270 theatres, 857 art galleries and four Unesco World Heritage sites. If you are wondering, they are the Tower of London, the Palace (and Abbey) of Westminster, Kew Gardens, and maritime Greenwich.

All this helps to explain why the London Convention Bureau, a division of the city’s official growth agency, is expecting close to 80,000 convention visitors this year. Thousands of rheumatologists and urologists have already been for their latest shindigs. The 44th World Scout Conference is due next year, along with hundreds of port and harbour delegates and a slew of tech conventions.

The striking thing is, the big draws for convention delegates are just a fraction of what London now offers its full-time residents.

As of this year, there is year-round outdoor swimming in, of all places, Canary Wharf. You can get there on the Elizabeth Line railway that has transformed cross-city travel. Or cycle there via the cycle superhighways that have revolutionised two-wheeled transport.

Or take the Tube that we all moan about constantly, and is admittedly expensive, but still zips you across the city in a sliver of the time it takes to cover such distances in other big cities. And you don’t even need to queue up for a ticket. Just swipe a credit card on the turnstile.

Next week, something even more astonishing will begin. After years of wrangling and false starts, a stretch of Oxford Street nearly 1km long will be closed to traffic as the famed shopping street at long last starts to become pedestrianised.

Is London ‘lawless’ or the safest big city in the western world? Take your pick

As usual, critics are predicting mayhem. Diverted traffic will clog side streets. Bin collections won’t work. People will feel unsafe at night, and so on.

I suspect the doubters will all be proved wrong and the move will be so successful that we will regret it not happening years ago.

At least I hope so. Watching a city brighten and improve is a pleasure for visitors and residents alike. At a time when war and political strife stalk ever more unlikely places, these are gains that should be celebrated – and never taken for granted. – Copyright The Financial Times

]]>Karl Hendon<![CDATA[‘A hovercraft I bought many years ago is still sitting in the same place as the day I got it’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/19/a-hovercraft-i-bought-many-years-ago-is-still-sitting-in-the-same-place-as-the-day-i-got-it/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/19/a-hovercraft-i-bought-many-years-ago-is-still-sitting-in-the-same-place-as-the-day-i-got-it/Mon, 19 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000James Hennessy is the founder of the National Reptile Zoo, based in Kilkenny, which works to advance environmental literacy, conservation practice and curiosity towards reptiles, amphibians, invertebrates and their habitats.

Are you a saver or a spender?

Definitely a spender. I’m also a firm believer that because you can’t take it with you when you’re gone, you need to enjoy it now, live in the moment and bring everyone along on the journey with you.

What was the first job you received money for, and how much were you paid?

I worked on a schoolfriend’s farm in primary school. It started out just helping out while hanging out with my friends. Eventually his dad would give me the occasional five pounds. They had a marsh on their land, and that’s probably where my obsession with frogs started to grow into my current obsession with all things slimy or scaly.

Do you shop around for better value?

Personally, I’d do lots of shopping around and research but equipment for the zoo tends to be very specialised. Unfortunately, there aren’t a lot of options when it comes to shopping around for that.

What has been your most extravagant purchase, and how much did it cost?

Two years ago, I bought an electric VW van for almost €60,000. It was a slightly worrying outlay at the time, but 100,000km later, it’s still going strong and is charged mostly by the solar array that we have on the roof.

What purchase have you made that you consider the best value for money?

In 2006, I bought a Toyota Hilux pickup. Almost three-quarters of a million kilometres on the clock later and I still have it. It has dragged building material and equipment around and has taken me on many adventures, and it’s still going strong. While we use the electric van mostly for work, I still have the Hilux for redundancy.

Is there anything you regret spending money on?

I bought a hovercraft many years ago, which is still in the same condition and sitting in the same position as the day I bought it.

Do you haggle over prices?

Only when I’m in a region where the culture allows for it. In Ireland, I have a very good grasp of the value of labour and materials; I don’t begrudge people trying to make a living and find it a bit insulting when people try to devalue someone’s labour or skills.

Do you invest in shares and/or cryptocurrency?

I don’t, mainly because I’ve not had enough exposure to it to have what I would consider a good enough grasp of it. I also prefer to see a more immediate return on any spare funds I might have.

Investing in cryptocurrency seems ‘like a more upmarket approach to gambling’

Do you have a retirement or pension plan?

I’ve got a very basic pension plan but I don’t have a plan to ever retire. As I become less able to work, I’d hope to be able to still potter about the place, giving some kind of input.

What was the last thing you bought, and was it good value for money?

I bought a vintage three-wheel car in the UK as a project car and drove it back to Ireland. The plan, as it is for a lot of these things for me, is to restore it, sell it and raise some funding. Is it good value for money? So far, I can neither confirm nor deny that.

Have you ever successfully saved up for a relatively big purchase?

Yes, quite a few. Big purchases are relative, of course. When I was around 12, I spent two years saving for a guitar, paying money into the guitar shop’s savings scheme each week.

Have you ever lost money?

Yes. I blew the engine in that vintage three-wheel car I recently bought.

The hard work and satisfaction in restoring classic cars: 'It's a learning process'

Are you a gambler and, if so, have you ever had a big win?

Not at all. While I will often take chances on purchases and business decisions, I don’t have any interest in betting. I see it as a bit pointless.

What is your best habit when it comes to money? And your worst?

My best habit is that I always tend to have a financial backup. While I enjoy living financially for the moment, I’ll always make sure I have that. My worst habit is impulse buying, and the stranger the purchase, the bigger the impulse.

How much money do you have on you now?

I always try to have some cash on me, so I have €45. It’s a good habit if you travel.

]]>LockieCurrie<![CDATA[Are many Irish homeowners undervaluing the cost of rebuilding their homes by €83,000?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/18/neglect-an-expensive-error-when-it-comes-to-insurance/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/18/neglect-an-expensive-error-when-it-comes-to-insurance/Sun, 18 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000There’s nothing like a big number to frighten consumers, especially when it comes to them being left out of pocket at a time of crisis.

Underinsurance can very quickly turn a drama into a financial crisis. Bad enough to have your home hit by flood, fire or other catastrophe without discovering your insurer will not cover the cost of putting things right.

People assume that if they have, say, €400,000 of insurance cover, any claim up to that value will be met. But that’s not the way it works.

If the cost of rebuilding your home is €600,000 but you only have cover for two-thirds of that (€400,000), the insurer will only cover two-thirds of every claim – even one for say €20,000 to repair flood damage – leaving homeowners thousands of euro out of pocket.

No one actually knows how pervasive the problem is.

Back in 2021, the Central Bank of Ireland sent a shot across insurers’ bows after a study by its staff discovered the level of underinsurance had surged from 6.5 per cent in 2017 to 16.5 per cent – not far short of 400,000 homes.

All increase the rebuilding cost in case of disaster, but the bank found that six in 10 homeowners never update their insurance details after investing to improve their homes.

With winter looming, now would be a good time to make sure you have the cover you think you have ... before anything goes wrong.

]]>Alamy<![CDATA[Elon Musk’s trillion-dollar pay deal has a convenient escape clause]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/18/musks-trillion-dollar-pay-deal-has-a-convenient-escape-clause/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/18/musks-trillion-dollar-pay-deal-has-a-convenient-escape-clause/Sun, 18 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000A million robotaxis, a million humanoid robots, and an $8.5 trillion valuation – Elon Musk’s trillion-dollar Tesla bonus appears to demand almost superhuman performance.

A recent study of executive pay finds that enormous share awards usually fail to deliver for shareholders and that “milestones are far less demanding than they appear”, with Musk’s 2025 Tesla package offering a striking illustration of the risks.

In Merging to the Moon: Astronomical Option Awards and Corporate Governance Failures, researchers examined 1.24 million insider stock awards between 1996 and 2022. They found that Tesla-style “mega-grants” subsequently underperformed comparable companies by 15 to 30 per cent over following years.

Tesla’s 2025 agreement offers Musk 424 million shares if the company reaches an $8.5 trillion market value and meets 12 demanding business milestones.

Considered in isolation, the package looks like a properly designed pay-for-performance deal. Under the researchers’ modelling, annual growth of 12 per cent in both Tesla’s share price and earnings would leave the company just short of its profits target after a decade.

If only one operational milestone was met (cumulative vehicle deliveries), Musk would get a payout of about $8 billion – a big sum, yes, but a fraction of the headline award.

However, if Tesla is acquired, the agreement completely waives the operational targets. If Tesla were taken over, the same share-price growth could deliver Musk $448 billion to $545 billion at a typical 20-30 per cent takeover premium, or up to about $707 billion at a 50 per cent takeover premium.

In other words, Musk could bag up to 88 times what he would earn on the operational track, without meeting a single operational goal.

Security teams usually want “every protection, every feature, all the way” but “at the same time, you have [recruiters] who say ‘this enhances friction for the candidate’”.

What sort of security checks are we talking about here? Recruitment platform Greenhouse has introduced a system to allow employers to prompt job seekers for ID verification. “Some do it at the top of the funnel, in the beginning of the process, and some do it further down,” Daniel Chait, Greenhouse’s chief executive, tells me.

Clarity, meanwhile, says it uses AI to examine “facial movements, lip-syncing, eye motions, voice patterns” and other indicators in video interviews, and cross-checks indicators such as “behavioural, identity, and media patterns” to spot signals of deception.

It sounds like a lot of personal data to be hoovered up in a process that might not even result in a job offer. There is surely the potential, too, for “false positives”: for legitimate candidates to be flagged as suspicious and thus denied the chance of getting hired. If a lot of employers start to use the same handful of systems, some unlucky souls might find themselves blocked again and again.

The good news is that the EU’s penchant for regulation has helped pre-empt some of these potential pitfalls. Both the General Data Protection Regulation directive and the European Union AI Act give people protection against being subject to unexplained automated decision-making, for example, especially in high-stakes areas such as recruitment.

Interviewing Gen Z teachers: A candidate told me I was in a bidding war for her

Both Wilf and Chait tell me their systems have been carefully designed to meet EU regulations and do not lead to automated decisions but only flag information for human review.

That said, these new security features and identity checks feel like a depressing consequence of the AI arms race in recruitment. Already, candidates complain they feel dehumanised by employers’ use of the technology, while employers say they can’t cope with the volume of AI-assisted applications.

According to Gartner’s regular surveys of job seekers, the number of people who had experienced an AI-led interview doubled from 9 per cent in the third quarter of last year to 18 per cent in the second quarter of this year. Have we reached the point where employers throw up their hands and go back to a much smaller pool of handwritten applications and in-person interviews?

It’s an appealing thought, but it’s worth remembering that way of doing things was hardly perfect either. Indeed, perhaps the worst-case scenario would be a future that contains a bit of both.

A return to more offline, human-to-human recruitment decisions for those who already have personal connections who can vouch for them (or those young people whose parents have connections). And for job seekers without that reserve of social capital? An interview into a webcam with three fingers pressed to your face. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

When budget changes kick in and how to claim them

You ask whether the transfer you are considering would be seen as a gift? It will, yes, but not one that is liable for gift tax.

At a practical level, you sensibly raise the issue of share certificates or, in more recent times, an electronic record of share ownership.

Registrars are companies that manage the share registers of listed companies. Most particularly, they keep track of who owns how many shares and record changes of ownership when shares are sold or otherwise transferred.

They also keep shareholders notified of company events, such as annual meetings, share placings, rights issues, consolidation, or special meetings to approve things like takeovers, etc.

There are a number of companies that specialise in this work. You do not identify which company’s shares we are talking about here so I cannot tell you which one you need to approach, but the information will be readily available in the investor relations section of the website of the company you’ve invested in.

You can also get the details from any email or letter they may have sent you.

They will send you a share transfer form to formalise the transfer of ownership of these shares to your wife. There will be a charge to do this. I cannot say precisely how much this will be but it tends to be fairly nominal.

If you do not have your share certificate, things can get a bit more costly as you may need to sign (and pay for) an indemnity letter.

Whoever succeeds her in owning these shares will not have to worry about the legacy capital gain dating back to the time you originally acquired the shares. Inheritance tax in Ireland: ‘The rules are absolutely skewed against the childless’

]]><![CDATA[Recent mergers may face investigation by regulators following Irish Government error]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/17/recent-mergers-may-face-investigation-following-government-error/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/17/recent-mergers-may-face-investigation-following-government-error/Sat, 17 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000Businesses that agreed mergers or takeovers in recent weeks may face investigation by competition regulators as a result of a Government mistake, it has emerged.

Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment, Peter Burke, increased the financial values at which mergers must be notified to the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) in July.

However, his department has confirmed that Burke’s order lapsed on September 30th, when it emerged that the Oireachtas had not approved it on time, exposing deals agreed or completed since that date to possible investigation by the commission.

The ministerial order increased the financial threshold at which mergers must be notified to the commission to a combined turnover of €100 million or more, from €60 million.

Competition law obliges the CCPC to investigate deals meeting the threshold to ensure they do not damage competition in their relevant markets, before approving them, often with conditions meant to protect competition.

As the order lapsed on September 30th, the old rules have applied since then.

So mergers or takeovers agreed or completed since then, where the parties’ combined turnover is €60 million or more, and two of those involved have sales of at least €10 million each, may face investigation by the commission.

The CCPC is advising businesses involved in transactions either agreed or completed since September 30th to consider if they meet the old threshold and whether they should notify it of the deal.

The commission pledged not to investigate any parties to deals done in those circumstances for “gun jumping”, that is completing the transactions before getting its approval.

Any mergers completed between July 1st and September 30th were subject to the increased threshold, that is a combined turnover of €100 million or more, and at least €15 million for two of the parties involved.

According to the department, Burke’s order increasing the threshold was laid before the Oireachtas, but did not get the approval of both the Dáil and Seanad within the time set out by the Competition Act, 2002.

“As a result, the order ceased to have effect,” said a spokeswoman, who confirmed that the error emerged following a department review.

The Act requires the CCPC to investigate mergers for their likely impact on competition, but gives the Minster the power to raise the thresholds for such inquiries to keep them in line with inflation and economic circumstances.

Ministerial orders, also dubbed statutory instruments, generally need Oireachtas approval before taking effect.

Burke signed the order on June 10th, branding the move part of his efforts to cut red tape for business.

The Minister said at the time that he increased the financial notification threshold in response to a public consultation that he held earlier this year.

The CCPC favoured an increase as it allowed the regulator to focus resources on deals more likely to have a meaningful impact on competition and consumers.

The last increase was in 2019, before the significant inflation that followed Covid and the war in Ukraine.

The commission has the power to “call in” transactions below the €100 million value where it believes they could affect competition.

The department will work with the CCPC to “progress revised merger notification thresholds at the earliest opportunity in 2027,″ according to its spokeswoman. The law allows only one change each year.

]]>Eddie Keogh/Imagination<![CDATA[From dereliction to Airbnb, the Gaeltacht is being destroyed by the housing crisis]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/10/17/the-gaeltacht-is-being-destroyed-because-we-wont-build-houses/https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/10/17/the-gaeltacht-is-being-destroyed-because-we-wont-build-houses/Sat, 17 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000As winter looms, the evening is so pitch black on Inis Meáin that the few street lights across the sea on Inis Mór make Kilronan look like Manhattan. Inis Meáin hosts one of the country’s few all-Irish boarding schools and it is full of life, always oversubscribed with teenagers enthusiastically embracing island life and its language. Tonight’s meeting is about what will happen in a few years, when these students – both locals and outsiders – become adults, and whether they can settle on the island, rear families, continue to speak Irish and infuse the community with vibrancy.

The impediment on Inis Meáin is housing. Irish-speaking adults who want to live here have few options as prices have gone through the roof for the tiny number of homes that come on the market. Meanwhile, restrictive planning laws mean locals cannot build new homes for their children on their plots.

Ireland’s islands are an essential part of Irishness, an integral part of our heritage and culture and one of the last bastions of Irish as a living, working, breathing, everyday language.

Tonight’s meeting is organised by a group of young Gaeilgeoirí activists called Tinteán (“níl aon tinteán mar do thinteán féin”), whose basic message is that if young Gaeilgeoirí can’t afford to live in the Gaeltacht, it will die very soon. Ironically, we are just a few hundred yards from the cottage where JM Synge spearheaded the Gaelic Revival.

Without people, there is no revival.

According to the latest census, the country’s island population has fallen below 3,000 for the first time. To put this into context, in 1841 there were 48,000 people living on the islands off the western seaboard. Today the average age on the islands is 59 - in contrast to the rest of the country, where it is 43 – and more than one in five of the islands’ population are aged 65 years and older.

The crucial age group between 20 and 35 accounts for just 7.9 per cent of the islands’ population, as opposed to 25 per cent for the State as a whole.

Meanwhile, just 5 per cent of the islands’ population is under four years old, compared with an average of 8 per cent nationally.

These population dynamics mean only one thing: catastrophic decline and, along with a disappearing population, a disappearing language and culture. What would Synge think?

It is essential that the population decline is reversed. At a time when the Irish language has rarely been more popular, when thousands of people are learning and in some cases relearning it, the Gaeltacht itself is being destroyed by the refusal to do the very thing that generations of people from the west of Ireland did all over the world: build houses. Young families make communities, and if they have no places to live then the community dies or becomes more like a museum – visited by curious onlookers during the holiday season, but for all intents and purposes, dead.

One of the main issues is that homes have become trophy assets. When a house here comes up for sale, it is marketed online to everyone from London to New York to Mount Merrion. There is a burgeoning national and international market for property in the west of Ireland, and this process elbows out the local people, pushing prices way out of reach for the average islander.

In addition, the tourist market, so long the source of summer income, has changed dramatically.

Airbnb and Booking.com have made it so attractive for property owners to rent out their places short term that these potential homes are taken off the rental market for young Gaeilgeoirí who can’t afford to compete in trophy auctions. In many cases they are being given the option to rent until the summer comes, and then weekly rents skyrocket for the tourist season and the families must find somewhere else to live until September. They are in effect school-year residents, and that oddly nomadic existence rarely encourages people to put down roots.

Naturally, as more and more rural hotels have been turned over to refugees, tourist bed capacity falls, putting more pressure on the existing housing stock.

Life on Inis Meáin: ‘Some people will say there’s nothing here, but in fact there is everything here’

Another issue is vacancy – and ultimately dereliction, because an uninhabited house doesn’t stand a chance against Atlantic storms for long. For example, according to the local community office, on Inis Meáin there are 149 houses, of which 65 are uninhabited. Nearly half of all the homes on an island with a housing crisis stand empty.

So what can be done?

We know that people respond to incentives, positive and negative. With respect to building houses in the Gaeltacht to enable Gaeilgeoir families to live here, the key is to create the incentives to make the local housing market work. Considering the fact that there are vacant houses on the island, what might make the owners put them on the market?

At the moment, capital gains must be paid if you sell a vacant property. This is an obvious impediment to selling. Why go through the hassle of selling, particularly an old family house split between a few children, if the government gets 31 per cent of the profit? What about specifically cancelling capital gains on the islands in order to lubricate supply? Make it easy to sell. Such a move would change the conversation about selling.

A buyer’s tax break, specifically for Gaeilgeoirí, like the Temple Bar tax breaks for residents in the 1990s, would bias buying to Irish speakers.

On the planning side, what about setting a quantity of homes to be built by locals every year, based on demand and family structure, allowing the residents to solve their own problems? This would give local people the ability to build on their own island, for their own community.

‘It’s just like a match made in heaven’: Family of seven who moved to Inis Meáin urge others to follow

Even if these initiatives were embraced, there is still the issue of the cost of island life – which is far in excess of anything on the mainland. Those of us who don’t live on small islands don’t realise that the sea is a big cost driver. Think about getting material to the island, renting the truck to bring the materials to the harbour on the mainland, renting the boat to bring the stuff across, finding the workers to do the job, putting them up while they are working, and so on. All these things cost money, yet the income of Ireland’s islanders is far below the national average.

What about making island life tax-free for Gaeilgeorí, treating the people the way we treat US multinational capital? When we cut corporation tax, activity responded. The same would apply with income tax, excise duty and VAT on islands.

If we are talking about the Gaeltacht and the language, what about making living on the island tax free for Gaeilgeori? The sums of money would be tiny for a country with an annual budget of €147 billion. We are talking about only a few thousand people initially. The cost is minuscule and the prize, the preservation of a way of life and a language that has been spoken continuously in this part of the country for more than 2,500 years, is enormous.

This morning I asked a local about the weather and he responded, “Tá sé leathghlas ceart go leor,” or, “It’s a bit half grey all right.” (Down here glas isn’t green, it’s grey.) The half grey refers to the sea, the sky and heavy clouds, and the colour of the rocks, the limestone and the horizon where the sea and the clouds meet in a misty angry grey haze. This linguistic richness comes from hundreds of generations inscribing their language with colour, significance and their own meaning.

Imagine losing this for the sake of a few pennies.

]]>Jade W <![CDATA[How Ireland’s first national public sector strike in 17 years left unions strong and Jack Chambers ‘scrambling’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/politics/2026/10/17/strike-success-leaves-unions-in-position-of-strength-and-jack-chambers-scrambling/https://www.irishtimes.com/politics/2026/10/17/strike-success-leaves-unions-in-position-of-strength-and-jack-chambers-scrambling/Sat, 17 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000Perhaps nobody in Government had heard the old sales business adage: the first one to name a price always loses.

But they might reflect now on how outlining a package aimed at public sector workers in last week’s budget ended up putting them on the back foot.

Within the trade union movement, some believe Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers was gambling that the Budget 2027 tax changes, along with the €1.2 billion set aside for public pay increases next year, would give the Government the upper hand going into talks.

Instead, union leaders seized upon the sums as something to publicly scoff at as, on Wednesday, their members took to the streets and formed picket lines in a public sector strike.

Chambers has been left to “scramble”, as one observer puts it, for several days, discounting all that has been offered so far as merely a starting point for the talks that will at some point follow this weekend’s preliminary engagement.

Labour TD Ged Nash suggested on Thursday, as he proposed a private members’ motion on the issue, that the Government had “sleepwalked” into a first national public sector strike in 17 years.

The sight of so many young workers who had never been on a picket line before outside their workplaces will have provided a wake-up call.

From a public relations perspective, the Government could have done without the parade of workers highlighting what they regard as its failings in interviews with the media.

Ciara Loftus, who works in the Mater’s emergency department, said she was still living at home at 25 and feels she has no chance of getting on the housing ladder. This was a recurring theme, along with childcare, among younger strikers.

“I feel like I’m going to be forced to move country by the end of the year or next year,” she said.

“It’s not sustainable.”

Across Dublin, in Dún Laoghaire, Conor Carroll, a porter at St Michael’s hospital, with young children at home, talked about being stung by food inflation whenever he visits the supermarket.

“You see the price of things,” he said, “even the stuff you need to eat. You’re just not earning enough these days.”

Maurice Sweeney, a lab worker at Trinity College Dublin, said he is supposed to be one of the lucky ones on what is considered a decent wage. The reality, he says, is different.

“The weekly shop has you under pressure and we didn’t see much benefit from that budget there last week at all,” he said.

Many expressed frustration to find themselves in this position when politicians keep telling them the country is booming.

During the last strikes, the situation was very different. Back in 2009, following the banking crisis and economic crash, workers walked out over the scale of the cuts made by a Government with no money and little scope for negotiation with unions.

A decade’s worth of talks and deals that followed, from 2010 to 2020, are characterised as “defensive” by one senior trade union leader.

Now, though, he suggests this week’s industrial unrest might have taken place six years ago, when the public sector pay deal entitled Building Momentum was negotiated, had it not been for the Covid pandemic and the huge uncertainty surrounding almost every aspect of work and the economy at the time.

Relations were strained then by what the unions regarded as the continued efforts by Department of Public Expenditure (DPER) officials to approach pay talks as though the country was still broke.

The situation has only been exacerbated by what they see as DPER’s vetoing, or delaying of, spending that unions thought they were entitled to. These frustrations extend to deals they say were already agreed, such as the local bargaining aspect of the last national pay agreement.

What made the situation significantly worse over the past year, contributing to the loss of trust for the unions, was the VAT cut to hospitality. This, they felt, was given based on arguments that would not stand up to the scrutiny their own spending proposals are subjected to. Then there was the Government caving to the demands of fuel protesters.

“What you had there,” says one observer on the union side, “was people who went, parked their tractors and trucks and said, ‘right, we have the country by the balls’.”

Another person with a vested interest points to “unelected people suddenly having access to the highest levels of Government and being able to force changes that in some cases had been agreed with elected representatives or people with a respect for democratic structures”.

“Say what you want,” says the first observer, “but unions are regulated, there are rules they have to observe and they do because of the potential consequences.”

Most workers – many in modestly paid jobs and feeling the pinch of rising grocery, fuel and accommodation costs – were more put out by the expiry of the last pay deal in June.

It came at a time when prices were on an upward trajectory but the Government had not indicated when they might get around to ensuring their wages were raised accordingly.

Predictably, there is now something of a blame game as to why talks on a new agreement were delayed beyond the expiry of the last deal in June. What is undisputed is that a couple of exploratory meetings in June went poorly.

By the time Chambers wrote an opinion article in The Irish Times on July 1st, he was suggesting “all issues of importance to both sides can and should be discussed as part of any engagement”. He also warned that “setting preconditions or barriers to engagement does not assist the process of building consensus and agreement”.

The unions indicated early on that they wanted to change what was regarded as the normal running order in previous negotiations and have pay addressed up front.

Fórsa’s Kevin Callinan and John Boyle of the Irish National Teachers’ Organisation have since said they believed pay increases had fallen between 5 and 7 per cent behind inflation over the previous four years. They wanted an agreed plan to close that gap over the lifetime of any new pay deal.

One of those familiar with the process on the Government side suggests the unions wanted a final outcome on the pay issue before anything else could be discussed.

This, they argue, would have left the negotiators on the employer side with no leverage at all as they sought improved productivity through changes to work practice around artificial intelligence (AI), hybrid working or anything else.

There seems to have been surprise among officials that the unions subsequently disengaged, as they viewed it, and proceeded to balloting on industrial action relatively quickly.

The unions express exasperation that Chambers did not intervene directly, pick up the phone or arrange to meet them.

Those with experience of previous pay-agreement negotiations suggest there would traditionally have been more going on by way of back channels.

Callinan’s repeated calls this week for Taoiseach Micheál Martin to get involved are likely rooted in this, it is suggested by veterans of the pre-crash system of engagement during the “social partnership” from 1987 to 2009. Martin, they observe, is the only survivor on the Government side of how that worked and they would like to see his department reassert the control it used to exert over the negotiations.

Martin taking over might not look good for Chambers. However, Callinan made it clear on Friday that the shape of the preliminary talks process was hammed over a call with the Taoiseach.

The unions believe they are in a good position as the process gets under way, given how well Wednesday’s strike went.

Michael Doherty, a professor of law at Maynooth University and a prominent figure in the industrial relations landscape, suggests “the Government may have got a shock by the number of young, enthusiastic people getting a first taste of industrial action on the pickets and anxious to be heard”.

Having energised this young and important constituency, he says the unions need to ensure they do not leave disappointed and disillusioned.

“They are going to have to be very careful because there is the possibility they won’t want to accept some sort of fudge, that they’ll feel, ‘Hold on, you marched us up the hill here’.”

At this juncture, the unions might have felt it was better to threaten a second strike date than carry through with another stoppage – especially on what is forecast to be a cold and rainy day next Wednesday.

Preventing the second strike should help Chambers and the Government to regain some control over the situation.

To get this far, he has repeatedly said that pay can be talked about at the outset, while the unions have stuck to their position: “Nothing is agreed until everything is agreed.”

Negotiating a deal that is good for the Government will still be a challenge, though.

Both sides point to different time periods, framing the relationship between pay and inflation in recent deals in a way that suits their purposes.

The unions do not want the sacrifices forced upon them in the wake of that strike 17 years ago to be written out of the equation.

Union leaders now talk about insuring their members against future spikes in inflation such as those caused by the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

However, such a mechanism would severely undermine the big prize from the negotiations for the Government: budgetary certainty for the coming few years.

The answer, some observers suggest, could be a short-term deal to get over the current impasse and allow everyone to come back when the tensions have eased. An alternative would be an agreement with a robust review clause for pay.

Both sides will likely agree on one thing if there is to be a short-term agreement: they will want to avoid being back in this current stalemate any sooner than they have to be.

]]>Don Moloney

   <title>Holzleitner verteidigt Unibudget</title>
   <description>Wissenschaftsministerin Eva-Maria Holzleitner (SPÖ) hat das Budget für die Universitäten am Sonntag in der ZIB2 verteidigt. <item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3445479/">

   <description>Der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj hat sich tief besorgt über eine mögliche Annäherung der USA an Russland geäußert. „Sollten sich die USA an die Seite Russlands stellen, können wir nicht überdauern“, sagte Selenskyj in einem Interview des Senders NBC am Sonntag zu den jüngsten Schritten von US-Präsident Donald Trump, wie etwa der Aussetzung von neuen Sanktionen.    <title>Macron verurteilt Gewalt bei Protesten</title>

Poland has condemned an attack by masked Israeli settlers on a delegation of European diplomats – including Polish ones – that was visiting the West Bank.

It called for a “decisive response from the Israeli authorities”, saying that the incident is “further evidence of the settler violence that the Palestinian population in the West Bank faces on a daily basis”.

The attack has likewise been condemned by France and Belgium, whose nationals were also in the delegation, and the European Union, as well as by the Israeli foreign minister.

Masked Israeli settlers attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, prompting European condemnation.

The violence comes amid unprecedented settler pogroms during the olive harvest. pic.twitter.com/wsP6edL62y

— Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) October 18, 2026

On Saturday, the delegation – which included members from France, Belgium and Poland as well as representatives of the Catholic church – visited the mostly Christian Palestinian village of Taybeh near Ramallah in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.

They had come to assess the situation following regular recent attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to harvest olives on their own land. During the visit, the delegation came under attack, with parts of the incident caught on camera.

France’s foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, reported that Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France, had been “violently assaulted” during the incident. He demanded that Israel arrest the perpetrators and “urgently put an end to these criminal acts of violence”.

 

Late on Saturday afternoon, the spokesman for Poland’s foreign ministry, Maciej Wewiór, issued a statement confirming that the attack had taken place and that the delegation had included an unspecified number of Polish diplomats, who he said had not been harmed.

“We express our deep outrage and strongly condemn this incident,” added Wewiór. “Poland consistently opposes violence by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank. Attacks on representatives of the diplomatic corps are absolutely unacceptable.”

The spokesman said that Poland now “expects urgent and detailed explanations from the Israeli authorities” and for the perpetrators of the attack to be identified and held accountable. “We also expect effective measures to prevent similar incidents in the future.”

❗Potwierdzamy, że na Zachodnim Brzegu Jordanu doszło do ataku na konwój, w którym znajdowali się przedstawiciele korpusu dyplomatycznego, w tym polscy dyplomaci. Według wstępnych informacji za atak mogą odpowiadać izraelscy osadnicy.
Polskim dyplomatom nic się nie stało. Z…

— Rzecznik MSZ – Maciej Wewiór (@RzecznikMSZ) October 17, 2026

On Sunday, Poland’s foreign ministry issued a further statement in which it “condemned the attack by masked settlers…during a solidarity visit to a town known for its centuries-old Christian presence”.

The incident “is further evidence of the settler violence that the Palestinian population in the West Bank faces on a daily basis”, they added, calling for a “decisive response from the Israeli authorities”.

The attack was also “strongly condemned” on Sunday by the European Union’s diplomatic service, which said that it “expects full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians”.

Belgium’s foreign minister, Maxime Prevot, said that his country would continue to “press for EU sanctions against those responsible for this violence and those who support them”.

🇵🇸 I condemn in the strongest terms the attack by masked settlers in Taybeh, in the occupied West Bank, against Palestinians, our Consul General, French and Polish diplomats as well as catholic representatives. A French mayor was assaulted and a Belgian vehicle damaged. Our team…

— Maxime PREVOT (@prevotmaxime) October 17, 2026

In the wake of the incident, Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu had urged people to show “caution before drawing conclusions” over what had happened. He claimed that there is “a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents” of the West Bank.

However, the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said that it “strongly condemns the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters”. But it added that “the consulate’s visit was not coordinated with the IDF”, which is “important to prevent incidents of this kind”.

Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, also issued a condemnation of the attack and said that police had opened an investigation.

The IDF strongly condemns the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters.

Police forces and forensic investigators from the Judea and Samaria District are entering the area accompanied by…

— Israel Defense Forces (@IDF) October 17, 2026

The incident involving the diplomatic group came a day after around 80 Israeli settlers had attacked Palestinians harvesting olives, with Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine among those injured.

Levine told the Committee to Protect Journalists, an American non-profit organisation, that she had been pushed to the ground by a group of masked settlers, who “were kicking me for I think at least 10 minutes”.

That incident prompted criticism of Israel from the United States, whose ambassador, Mike Huckabee, called it a “despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards”.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, said he was “disturbed” by the incident and confirmed that “we’ve asked the Israelis to crack down on that”.

.@SecRubio on reporter Heidi Levine being attacked in the West Bank: "We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing….the President has been very clear, he's said this repeatedly, he does not want to see friction or crisis going on in the West Bank." pic.twitter.com/Xg10vteeXK

— CSPAN (@cspan) October 18, 2026

In August this year, Poland summoned Israel’s ambassador to express its “great disappointment” that the IDF had discontinued an investigation into the strikes on an aid convoy in Gaza in 2024 that killed seven humanitarian workers, including a Pole, Damian Soból.

In May, Poland issued a five-year entry ban on Israeli national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir for his treatment of detained activists, including Polish citizens, from a flotilla seeking to reach Gaza.

Last year, Israel criticised Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, after he suggested that Israeli politicians are causing the starvation of mothers and children in Gaza. The Israeli foreign ministry called the remarks “unacceptable” and urged Tusk to “remember the lessons” of the Holocaust.

Many more municipalities in Poland will be allowed to charge a daily fee for tourists and other overnight visitors after a change to the law dropping environmental requirements for levying such charges.

Kraków, which received 8.7 million overnight tourists last year, had in particular been pushing for the change. However, Poland as a whole has seen a recent boom in visitor numbers, recording the EU’s second-fastest growth in the number of nights in tourist accommodation last year.

#Krakow #opłataturystyczna #ustawa 🚨🔥Z OSTATNIEJ CHWILI! 🔥🚨

📢 Prezydent RP podpisał nowelizację przepisów dotyczących podatków i opłat lokalnych, PIT oraz PCC.

🏨 Najważniejsze zmiany dla branży turystycznej dotyczą opłaty miejscowej i uzdrowiskowej.

🗓️ Od 2027 r. za jej… pic.twitter.com/9ATvENvNol

— Kraków (@krakow_pl) October 15, 2026

Until now, a “visitor’s fee” could be levied by municipalities with beneficial climatic features, “scenic qualities” and the capacity to accommodate people visiting to benefit from these attributes, as well as localities in areas with the status of a “spa protection area”. In practice, this largely applied to seaside and mountain resorts.

Kraków did charge a visitor’s fee between 2004 and 2015, but was subsequently unable to do so due to a toughening of environmental requirements. The city has long suffered from bad air pollution, though it has taken significant steps to tackle the issue.

Now, under new legislation proposed by the government earlier this year and signed into law by President Karol Nawrocki this week, the requirement for beneficial climatic features has been scrapped, meaning many more places will be able to charge the visitor’s fee.

 

From 1 January, municipalities with scenic qualities will be able to charge visitors up to 5 zloty (€1.14) for each night they stay in hotels, guesthouses and short-term rental accommodation for up to one month, a rise on the current maximum of 3.46 zloty.

Additionally, whereas previously only people visiting for the purposes of tourism had to pay, the fee now applies to all visits, including for work or health purposes, reports broadcaster TVN. People with significant disabilities, children with certified disabilities and their carers will be exempt from the fee.

In another change, fees will be collected directly by accommodation providers, who will be required to maintain detailed records, reports the Infor news service. Passing fees on in a timely manner will entitle providers to receive at least 10% of the money they collect.

Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026

In 2024, Kraków appealed to the government to be allowed to charge tourists a fee, noting that “overtourism leads to tensions and social discontent”, as the “local community suffers” and “residents increasingly feel like tourists in their own city”.

With its UNESCO-listed Old Town, Wawel royal castle, and former Jewish district of Kazimierz, Kraków is regularly named as one of Europe’s best tourist destinations. Last year, a record 16.25 million people visited the city, of whom 8.7 million stayed overnight.

While that is a boon to the local economy, it also often causes tensions with residents, who complain about noise and disruption. In 2024, the city created the new position of “night mayor”, whose role is to reconcile the needs of tourists, businesses and residents.

Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals of the type offered through services such as Airbnb.

Such accommodation has boomed in recent years, often prompting a backlash from local residents https://t.co/8MRfRWTDxd

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 3, 2026

Following this week’s change to the law, Kraków city hall confirmed that it would now again be able to collect a visitor’s fee “if the statutory conditions are satisfied and the municipal council adopts an appropriate resolution”.

The city’s recently elected new mayor, Łukasz Gibała, who will be sworn in next week, said before Sunday’s election that he was in favour of a tourist tax of at least 20 zloty per night, four times the new maximum.

“In western European cities there are rates of that size and higher,” Gibała said, quoted by financial news service Money.pl. “Maintaining the city in the face of the influx of tourists is costly. In Kraków, private business owners profit from tourism, whilst the city and its residents foot the bill.”

Poland as a whole has also experienced a boom in tourism. Last year, the country recorded the European Union’s second-largest growth in the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation. Its increase of 7% was behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta (9.9%).

Poland’s interior ministry has withdrawn a proposal to make it a criminal offence, punishable by up to three years in prison, to provide support to migrants who are in the country illegally. The idea had prompted criticism from human rights groups and even opposition from within the government.

The interior ministry said the amendment had been intended to clamp down on migrant smuggling. But activists feared it would criminalise humanitarian aid, such as that provided to migrants who have irregularly crossed the border from Belarus.

By Daniel Tilles

Poland will hold parliamentary elections a year from now. The outcome will decide who governs the country for the next four years – although, given how close the polls are, and with questions over coalition formation, it could also result in uncertainty, chaos, and even new elections being called.

Below, we explain how the elections work, which parties will be standing, what kind of outcomes are possible, and which issues may animate the campaign.

When will the election take place?

Assuming early elections are not called, the vote must take place on a non-working day in the last 30 days before the end of the current four-year parliamentary term, which began on 13 November 2023.

Because elections in Poland are held on Sundays, that gives four possible dates: 17, 24 or 31 October, or 7 November (though 1 November and 11 November, which are public holidays, are also theoretically possible).

It is the president, Karol Nawrocki, who will choose the date. He must do so no later than 90 days before the end of the current parliamentary term.

How does voting work?

The 460 members of the more powerful lower house, the Sejm, are elected through proportional representation, meaning that seats are distributed more or less on the basis of the share of the vote parties receive (using the so-called D’Hondt method for allocating seats from electoral lists put forward by each party). However, parties must receive at least 5% of the vote nationally to enter parliament (a figure that rises to 8% for coalitions of parties who stand on a single electoral list).

The 100 members of the upper-house Senate are chosen through a first-past-the-post system similar to how members of the US Congress or British House of Commons are elected, with the candidate in each district that receives the most votes winning the seat.

How is a government formed?

A government can only be formed if it can win a vote of confidence in the Sejm.

After the elections, the president designates a prime minister, who is tasked with forming a government – which would almost certainly be made up of a coalition of parties – that must then win a vote of confidence.

If they fail to do so (as happened in 2023), the Sejm votes to choose an alternative prime minister, who likewise must try to form a government that has the confidence of the Sejm.

Parliament has chosen @donaldtusk as Poland's new prime minister.

That paves the way for him to form a new government in the coming days, ending the eight-year rule of the national-conservative PiS party https://t.co/iZUKh2rxnP

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 11, 2023

If that fails, the president has a second chance to pick a prime minister, who must again win a confidence vote. However, whereas the previous two votes require an absolute majority (większość bezwzględna) to be carried, this time only a simple majority is needed, making it easier to form a minority government.

If this third and final attempt does not work, then parliament is dissolved and new elections are called.

Who is likely to form the next government?

At the moment, it is incredibly difficult to say. Polls suggest an even split in support between parties generally aligned with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition – which ranges from left to centre right – and the right-wing opposition. However, the 5% electoral threshold complicates the picture.

According to current polling averages compiled by Polish website eWybory and Politico Europe, Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) leads with 32%. One of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), is on 7%, while two others, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), are on around 3% and 1%, respectively. Another left-wing party, Together (Razem), which previously caucused with the ruling coalition but split in 2024, is on around 4%.

Meanwhile, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, is on 20%. Two far-right opposition groups, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have 14% and 9%, respectively. The right-wing Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which broke away from PiS this year, is at around 5%.

Rolling 30-day average support in polls for Poland’s main political parties (source: eWybory.eu)

If we treat those as two potential blocs, parties more or less aligned with the current government are on around 47% while the right-wing opposition is on 48%. However, PSL and Poland 2050 currently look likely to fall below the 5% threshold if they stand alone, meaning votes for them would not count. That would significantly harm Tusk’s chances of forming a new government. If Rozwój Plus stood alone and fell below the threshold, that would harm the opposition.

It is therefore likely that, as the elections draw nearer, parties that seem likely to fall below 5% will seek to join forces with other groups. In 2023, PSL and Poland 2050 stood together in the so-called Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance. But they have made clear they do not intend to do that again. That leaves them with limited options. They could join forces with KO on a single electoral list, but that does not guarantee that their voters will follow them. Indeed, some may baulk at voting for Tusk’s party.

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026

Meanwhile, there are some wildcards in the pack. KKP, led by radical-right extremist Grzegorz Braun, is shunned by the mainstream right for its antisemitism, anti-Americanism and sympathy towards Russia. PiS’s leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, has declared that he would not allow Braun to join government. Development Plus has taken a similar position. Both parties value relations with the US and the Trump administration, whose ambassador to Poland has reportedly pushed them to rule out working with Braun.

However, if KKP maintains its current level of support, it looks almost impossible for the opposition to form a parliamentary majority without it, meaning there would be a strong temptation to somehow work with Braun. Kaczyński’s determination to remove Tusk from power may outweigh his dislike of Braun and desire to keep the Americans onside.

The Together party – if it manages to pass the 5% threshold – could likewise represent a challenge for Tusk when forming a coalition, given that it has criticised the government for failing to keep promises on healthcare spending, public sector pay, and liberalising the abortion law.

 

There also remains the possibility of some elements from each camp joining the other side – either entire parties or individual MPs defecting – in order to help form a government.

PiS has long sought to tempt PSL to its side (and recent reports suggest that even President Donald Trump tried to persuade PSL’s leader, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, to do so). It is conceivable that Rozwój Plus could work with parts of the current ruling camp, though its hatred of Tusk would make that very difficult.

All of the difficulties outlined above mean there is a significant chance that it will not be possible for anyone to form a government, necessitating fresh elections – something that has never happened before in Poland. If that happens, it would mean uncertainty and a lack of clear leadership at a time when Poland is facing major security challenges and a worsening fiscal situation.

What about the Senate?

The Senate, like the Sejm, is currently controlled by the ruling coalition. Indeed, Tusk has an even larger majority there than in the lower house, making it harder for the opposition to flip. Although the Senate is much weaker than the Sejm – and control of it does not determine who forms the government – it does have some powers that make it a useful asset.

It can slow down the passage of legislation, though not block it. The Senate also must approve the appointment of certain officials, such as the heads of the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) and the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), as well as the Commissioner for Human Rights (RPO).

The upper house is also required to approve proposals by the president to hold national referendums. This year, the Senate has twice blocked moves by Nawrocki to hold a referendum on EU climate policies.

In a situation where Tusk’s coalition controlled the Sejm, and was therefore still in government, but the right-wing opposition held the Senate, that would give the president a powerful tool to call referendums on policies important to him and the opposition.

To that end, there have been calls for the right-wing and far-right opposition to form a so-called Senate pact, of the type that Tusk and his allies used to win control of the upper house in 2019 and 2023.

What that means in practice is that the parties forming the pact agree to stand only one candidate between them in each of the 100 Senate districts, making it more likely that they will scoop up votes from supporters of all the parties in the pact and win the winner-takes-all contest.

What role will Nawrocki play in all of this?

Presidents are in theory expected to be non-partisan. In practice, however, they will seek to boost parties or coalitions aligned with them, and with whom it will be easier to work.

Since Nawrocki was elected last year, relations and cooperation between the president and government have reached unprecedently low levels. Within just 10 months, Nawrocki had vetoed more bills than any previous president in history over their entire terms. He has made it abundantly clear that he would prefer to work with a government formed from the right-wing opposition.

During his first year, President Nawrocki has transformed his office into a centre of resistance to the government and become a unifying figure for the fragmented right.

In practical terms, this could involve him acting as the patron of a Senate pact (something the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet recently said the president was willing to do), as well as helping right-wing parties form a coalition government after the elections.

Nawrocki also continues to enjoy strong approval ratings among the conservative electorate, meaning that his presence during the election campaign could act as a boost for the opposition.

What issues are likely to feature in the campaign?

A major issue will be the question of sovereignty. The right-wing opposition accuses Tusk of being Brussels’ and Berlin’s lapdog, handing over ever more power to the EU and prioritising Germany’s interests over Poland’s.

The ruling coalition, meanwhile, argues that PiS is too beholden to the Trump administration and warns that the opposition is pushing Poland towards “Polexit” from the EU, which would leave the country isolated and vulnerable, as well as much poorer.

Those battle lines extend to security policy too, with the Tusk government shifting emphasis towards Europe as a defence partner but PiS insisting that only the US can truly guarantee Poland’s security. Poland’s desire to host a new permanent US military base has already become highly politicised. If progress stalls, the opposition will blame the government. If Washington confirms that the base will go ahead, Nawrocki will seek to take the credit, based on his good relationship with Trump.

On this point, though, it is worth noting the split within the opposition. While PiS and Rozwój Plus are strongly pro-American, Confederation and, to an even greater extent, KKP, are opposed to a greater US presence in Poland.

In one of his first policy announcements since being elected on Sunday, the new mayor of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has declared that he will withdraw official patronage of its annual LGBT+ equality march.

Łukasz Gibała, who has been supportive of LGBT+ rights in the past and has previously attended the march, argues that the event has become too “partisan”. He stood for election as an independent and has pledged to depoliticise city hall.

His decision does not prevent the march from taking place. But it means that it no longer has the official support of the city.

Kraków’s equality march, which was first held in 2004, draws thousands of participants when it takes place each year in May. The event is used to demand greater LGBT+ rights in Poland, which is ranked as one of the worst countries in Europe for LGBT+ people.

In 2021, the city’s former mayor, Jacek Majchrowski, became an honorary patron of the march. In 2024, his successor, Aleksander Miszalski, became the first mayor to attend the event, declaring that Kraków should be “a home for everyone”.

However, Miszalski was removed from office earlier this year in a recall referendum, necessitating a new election, which was won by Gibała. He beat Monika Piątkowska, who, like Miszaski, is a member of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

The day after his victory, Gibała was asked by local broadcaster Radio Kraków if he would continue city hall’s patronage of the equality march. The new mayor, who takes office next week, declared that he would not, saying he “will avoid sponsoring events that have a partisan character”.

“I have the impression that, over the past three years or so, the community that organises equality marches has simply become partisan,” said Gibała. “These are people who ran for parliament and local government on the lists of specific political parties.”

Gibała did not indicate who he was referring to. However, one of the organisers of the equality march in Kraków is Magdalena Dropek, who has three times stood as a candidate for The Left (Lewica), one of the groups in Tusk’s ruling coalition, in elections to the Polish and European parliaments.

 

Gibała emphasised that he has himself attended equality marches in the past “and does not regret it”. He was previously an MP for both KO (when it was known as Civic Platform, PO) as well as for the liberal Palikot’s Movement (Ruch Palikota), later known as Your Movement (Twój Ruch).

During the recent mayoral election campaign, Gibała told broadcaster TVN that, as an MP, he had supported the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships in Poland, and said that his views had not changed.

When asked if that meant that, as mayor, he would continue the city’s practice of transcribing foreign same-sex marriages into the civil registry – as Poland was ordered to do last year by the Court of Justice of the European Union – Gibała said that he would.

However, he added that he was doing this as a “legalist” who respects the current legal situation. “If a different political party wins [parliamentary elections] next year and changes the law in Poland, it [recognition of foreign same-sex marriages] won’t happen,” he told Radio Kraków.

In fact, although the current government supports recognition of foreign-same sex marraiges, it has not changed the law in that regard. Polish law still does not recognise any form of same-sex union.

The government, aware that opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki would veto any change to the law, instead issued a regulation (which does not require presidential approval) empowering local authorities to transcribe foreign same-sex marriages into their registries.

Many municipalities, especially more liberal larger cities, have begun to do so (some even did before the regulation was issued). But others, especially in more conservative places, have refused to, often arguing that there are legal doubts around the issue.

Data provided to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) by the digital affairs ministry last week showed that 516 foreign same-sex marriages have so far been registered in Poland. The largest numbers were in Warsaw (209), Wrocław (73) and Kraków (46).
