The standoff between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki over Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom Prime Minister Donald Tusk recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president.

Berek is now the fifth judge to take their oath without presidential approval. The previous four have been denied entry to the TK, and speculation is rife that the government may soon take action to ensure that the excluded judges are able to take up their positions.

PILNE 🚨 dr Maciej Berek złożył w Sejmie ślubowanie na sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego! pic.twitter.com/sZlzLnsL3M

— Bogdan Zdrojewski (@BZdrojewski) October 14, 2026

Under Polish law, a new TK judge must swear an oath “before the president”. However, since Berek was elected to the TK by the government’s majority in parliament in early September, Nawrocki has refused to swear him in.

The president claims that Berek has not presented evidence that he meets the statutory requirement of having practiced as a legal counsel for at least 10 years. Berek says he has done so.

Nawrocki has also expressed his opposition to the fact that Berek has gone from serving in Tusk’s cabinet, where he was minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of policy, to becoming a TK judge.

Even some members of Tusk’s ruling coalition opposed Berek’s candidacy, saying that it contradicted the government’s earlier pledges to “depoliticise” the judicial system, including by banning anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge.

 

With no invitation from Nawrocki forthcoming, on Wednesday morning Berek instead swore his oath at a ceremony organised in parliament. He declared that he was directing the oath towards the president, despite Nawrocki not being present.

The development came a day after the Venice Commission, an advisory body to the Council of Europe on constitutional law, had issued an opinion effectively supporting the government’s position on the crisis around the TK.

The commission found that the Polish president should swear in TK judges chosen by parliament “without delay” and does not have the power to review their election. It added that, if the president refuses to receive a judge’s oath, they are justified in taking it without him being present.

The opinion was welcomed by Tusk and his government. However, Nawrocki’s spokesman, Rafał Leśkiewicz, pointed out that the Venice Commission’s opinions are advisory and not legally binding.

Rising mortgage rates are starting to “bite harder” on the UK’s fragile housing market by forcing sellers to push down asking prices. The average two-year fixed mortgage rate has risen to 5.55 per cent, up from 5.29 per cent last month and 4.25 per cent since before the war in Iran, according to homes portal [...]]]>

Rising mortgage rates are starting to “bite harder” on the UK’s fragile housing market by forcing sellers to push down asking prices.

The average two-year fixed mortgage rate has risen to 5.55 per cent, up from 5.29 per cent last month and 4.25 per cent since before the war in Iran, according to homes portal Rightmove.

Prices for properties put on sale on the site in October were one per cent higher than the month before, at £371,015, but the group says it is seeing signs that the housing market is starting to weaken. 

This one per cent price growth is below the 1.3 per cent average for October, a month when asking prices typically rise. Prices are virtually flat compared to a year ago, down 0.1 per cent.

Colleen Babcock, a property expert at Rightmove, said rising mortgage rates are “really beginning to hit buyers’ budgets” by forcing sellers to keep prices down. 

“It’s an early sign that higher mortgage costs are putting pressure on affordability even in markets with lower property prices, affecting the areas and types of property that buyers can afford.”

In London, where higher home values mean taxes like stamp duty weigh more heavily on buyers, house prices are 1.7 lower than the same time last year. 

Asking prices in the capital saw the biggest regional month-by-month jump in October, up 2.5 per cent, though London remains the weakest performing area of the UK. 

Tom Bill, head of residential research at property firm Knight Frank, said: “Prices will continue to be squeezed in the final months of the year as higher mortgage costs due to the Middle East conflict increasingly weigh on buyers. 

“Uncertainty around the familiar list of potential property tax hikes in the Budget is aggravating the situation.”

Housebuilders under pressure

Separate research from estate agency Hamptons has shown that most first-time buyers are now paying more on their mortgage than they did on rent. 

Brits who moved into their first home from rented accommodation last month were paying an average of £1,266 per month on mortgage repayments, compared to the £1,277 they had been spending on rent.

“The long-term benefits of home ownership – building equity, greater security and eventually owning a home outright – remain, but the immediate monthly saving that once rewarded tenants for making the leap has largely disappeared,” said Aneisha Beveridge, head of research at Hamptons.

Anthony Codling, an analyst at RBC Capital Markets, said Rightmove’s new data “reinforces a challenging operating environment” for the UK’s housebuilders, which have been battling with dampened demand and rising supply costs due to the Middle East conflict. 

Shares in London’s listed housebuilders rocketed at the end of last month after Andy Burnham announced the revival of Help to Buy equity loan scheme for first-time buyers.

Analysts said the buoyant market response to the announcement showed that the sector was in need of a stimulus, though they warned builders will still struggle in the absence of supply-side support. 

Top housebuilders Taylor Wimpey and Berkeley have hit out at London’s housebuilding market in recent weeks, warning planning objections are beginning to make building in the capital unviable.

Brits playing music out loud on a bus could be slapped with a £100 fine as part of Andy Burnham’s new crackdown on antisocial behaviour. 

Bus and train passengers will be asked to “share the carriage, not the noise” as part of new powers being handed to local authorities to clamp down on “the actions of an inconsiderate few”. 

The Prime Minister has encouraged councils to use new powers to crack down on loud music, littering, vaping and threatening behaviour on public transport. 

Local authorities have been handed new powers to levy fixed penalty notices of £100 on bus passengers playing loud music, though these new rules will need to be signed off by the transport secretary. 

Transport secretary Heidi Alexander said: “It is so frustrating when the actions of an inconsiderate few spoil journeys for the rest of us, whether that is vaping, littering or blasting music out loud.

“Even small changes in behaviour can make a massive difference to people’s experience on public transport.”

The government is issuing guidance to encourage councils to use new powers, introduced in August this year, to crackdown on antisocial behaviour on buses. 

Bus drivers will not be responsible for enforcing the new rules, the government said. This will be left to transport safety officers and the police.

‘Nobody wants pounding techno’

The government is also launching a new campaign to remind train passengers that they could face a fine of up to £1,000 for refusing to stop playing music aloud, according to existing rules.

Burnham said: “We’ve all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey.

“So, we’re launching a nationwide campaign reminding passengers to use headphones on trains. It’s a simple thing, but one that will make journeys that little bit better for all of us.”

Richard Holden, the shadow transport secretary, said Labour is “finally catching up with the Conservatives on issues passengers really care about”. 

“After we led the charge against antisocial behaviour on public transport last summer, ministers have worked out that nobody wants to endure pounding techno or blaring hip hop on a packed train or bus,” he added. 

Holden said the government should now crack down on the “far more serious problems” facing public transport passengers and staff, like aggressive behaviour. 

Assaults against rail staff have increased by 68 per cent under the Labour government while prosecutions have slumped, the Tory shadow minister said.

Microsoft has pulled out of plans to build the UK’s largest AI data centre in a deal with Nscale.

The global tech giant, which had previously planned to fund a supercomputer at the site, has ended its involvement in the partnership leaving Nscale scouting for alternative power resources.

Plans were first announced last year, with Nscale pledging £2bn to build and open a pioneering facility in Loughton, Essex. The government hailed the agreement at the time with former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer highlighting the project in the UK’s AI strategy in 2025.

But concerns surrounding power supplies has led to Microsoft, which was being viewed as the anchor tenant for the centre, pulling the plug on its end of the deal.

“Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term,” Nscale said, despite Microsoft’s withdrawal, which was first reported by The Telegraph.

The two firms are engaged in tie-ups across Europe and the United States.

Nscale heading for blockbuster listing

Nscale, which was founded in London, is backed by global tech giants including Nvidia and has positioned itself as Britain’s “sovereign” datacentre.

The loss of Microsoft on the Loughton project hands a timely blow to the firm as it gears up for a blockbuster listing in New York.

It is planning to list on the New York Stock Exchange – with a target valuation of reportedly up to $35bn – while maintaining its British domicile.

The London-based firm, which has former deputy prime minister Nick Clegg and former Meta executive Sheryl Sandberg as members of its board, reported a net of loss of $1bn on revenues of $141m in the first half of the year, with the bulk of losses caused by non-cash charges.

In March the group was valued at roughly $14.6bn in a funding round led by Norwegian energy group Aker and 8090 industries. Nvidia, Dell and Nokia also participated in the round.

Microsoft was contacted for comment.

    Facing allegations of racism, bigotry and sexism, can Nigel Farage clean up Reform UK’s act? It’s not even clear that he wants to, writes Eliot Wilson

    The news that a year-long undercover investigation by ITV News has revealed racism, bigotry and sexism among a number of Reform UK’s candidates and office-holders was not a surprise. This problem has deep roots.

    Former currency trader and hotelier Catherine Blaiklock established the Brexit Party, out of which Reform UK grew, with Nigel Farage’s support in January 2019. She lasted exactly two months as its leader before Farage took over, after she was revealed to have written and retweeted racist social media posts. Her own work included “Islam = submission – mostly to raping men it seems” and “I want my country back. I want seaside donkeys on the beach and little village churches, not acid attacks, mobs and mosques”. She also retweeted 45 posts by Mark Collett of the BNP including a caption of a photograph of a classroom of multiracial pupils which read “This is a British school. This is white genocide.”

    During the last general election campaign, the party had to disassociate itself from three parliamentary candidates. One accused immigrants from sub-Saharan Africa of “diluting” the UK’s collective IQ and another said black people should “get off [their] lazy arses” and stop acting “like savages”. A third responded to news of a boat carrying illegal migrants landing at Dover by saying, “I hope I’m near one of the scumbags one day I won’t run away I’ll slaughter them then have their family taken out”.

    At the time, Farage defended his party by claiming it had been “so desperate for people to stand that people stood, and then we employed a big vetting company who didn’t do the job”. He also argued that Reform UK had “an awful lot of candidates being stitched up in the most extraordinary way, with quotes taken out of context”.

    Reform faces fresh revelations

    Last week’s documentary, ITV Exposure—Undercover: A Year in Reform, was more comprehensive but wholly recognisable. Alan Feeley, a Reform UK councillor in Solihull, described Asian people as “absolute parasites” and wanted the authorities to “drag them out of their homes, stick them on planes and f*** them off to Pakistan”. He expressed the belief that “no more than one per cent of British population can be non-white”.

    Dean Miller, a councillor in Bromley, played fast and loose with the Treason Act 1351 when he said: “Apparently, King Charles is a fucking Muslim.. cut the cunt’s head off”. He claimed that immigrants had “come to rape and pillage and fucking kill us”, and that white people had “been ethnically cleansed out of London”. He added, “Like all the ethnic fucking kids, they’re not white, they’re all fucking black, and they’re like fucking animals. It’s horrible to say it. I’m not racist.”

    The response of Reform UK and its leader to these accusations has been predictable and rote. A statement said that “from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting. This is the same for all organisations”. However, the party claims to have “improved and prioritised its vetting procedures”, a promise Farage made more than two years ago. It has seemingly not been especially successful.

    Attack is the best form of defence. Reform UK also criticised ITV’s “extreme methods of deception”. Richard Tice, the party’s deputy leader, alleged that one figure was “a Tory plant” who was “deliberately saying some things to make us look bad”. Reform UK may not need much assistance in that area. There were also accusations of entrapment, although it is not clear how people who are not racist are so easily “entrapped” into making such enthusiastically racist remarks.

    Robert Jenrick, the former pro-Remain, centrist Conservative MP who managed to be dropped from Cabinet for lapses of propriety by Boris Johnson, dismissed the most recent allegations against Reform UK as “bad apples”. He misunderstands the proverb. It does not show that every sample has a few sub-standard elements; rather it warns that one malign presence can be corrosive to a whole group, or, as was more pithily written in 1340, “a rotten apple quickly infects its neighbour”.

    Can Reform UK ever be a serious party?

    Reform UK, despite seeming to be running out of momentum in opinion polls, attempts to present itself as a serious potential party of government. It cannot do so with any credibility while racists are dismissed as bad apples, vague promises are made of improved vetting procedures, accusations of serious financial impropriety are brushed aside by a smirking Farage and the party’s fundamental and universal defence is “a big boy did it and ran away”.

    Nigel Farage is probably the most influential British politician of the 21st century so far, and he has proven himself often a brilliant campaigner. But he is not a leader of a party. He has carved out a 30-year career as the carney barker for a shifting coalition of the aggrieved: anti-EU, anti-immigration, anti-woke, anti-lockdown, anti-net zero. You cannot build a political party on the platform of “Fings Ain’t Wot They Used T’Be”.

    There will be a general election in less than three years; less than three months, if some rumours are to be believed. The window is closing for Farage to demonstrate that he can turn Reform UK into a political party in a meaningful sense, and that he wants to. The jury is out on both counts.

    Eliot Wilson is a writer and historian. He is a senior fellow for national security at the Coalition for Global Prosperity and a contributing editor at Defence on the Brink

    Firms may be reluctant to admit when AI goes wrong, but industries like aviation show why sharing those near misses matters, writes Freya Russell

    Embarrassment originates from the French embarrasser, which more literally translates as “to block”. When it comes to safer AI, embarrassment does just that: it blocks a golden opportunity to share for the greater good. 

    When AI makes a mistake, no matter how small or large, if it is caught before it reaches a client, the natural inclination is to sweep the near miss under the carpet. There has been no harm to the firm, and admitting a mistake can invite consequences that extend far beyond the original error. So, why would a firm admit to such a narrow escape? The premise is that they would if the repercussions of a confession were to be removed.

    AI is already embedded in financial services; HM Treasury reports that 75 per cent of financial services firms are already using AI in at least one business function. With each implementation comes new lessons: areas where AI performs poorly, where human judgement was needed and what controls prevented a mistake. The number of these experiences is considerable, yet we are failing to do anything with them. Collectively, these present an opportunity for industry-wide progress. 

    Aviation: A model for reporting mistakes

    Financial services has an opportunity to follow a precedent set by the aviation sector decades ago. Celebrating its 50th anniversary this year, NASA’s Aviation Safety Reporting System has collected more than 2.3m voluntary, confidential reports, which are analysed and shared with the wider aviation community. One airline’s experience can help another avoid making the same mistake. HM Treasury is now proposing that financial services apply this principle to AI through a confidential, voluntary repository for reporting AI incidents and near misses.

    Making the repository confidential is a step in the right direction; having the incidents and remedies limited to a select group reduces the risk of fallout. However, the issue of embarrassment remains. Research in the Journal of Business Ethics on risk reporting in financial services found that “fear, embarrassment, guilt… should not be understated”. This shame is not merely an individual emotion; it can become an organisational incentive to keep quiet. For the repository to be a success, a more ambitious approach is needed. Chatham House Rules would reduce the reputational risk of speaking openly; if this measure were in place any addition to the repository could not be traceable to a particular firm. With the embarrassment factor eliminated, the next hurdle the proposal faces is perhaps more fundamental. 

    Where does competitive advantage end, and where does collective resilience begin?     Profit warnings from London listed businesses reached the highest levels in nearly two years over the summer, as an energy shock brought on by the Iran war fuelled inflation.

    Businesses issued 65 profit warnings during the period, up from 59 in the second quarter, according to the latest analysis from EY. It also marked the largest number of warnings since the fourth quarter of 2024, when 71 were issued.

    Profit warnings are announcements to shareholders informing them that initial market forecasts on profit or earnings will not be met.

    Over half of companies blamed the rise on geopolitical uncertainty, with 38 per cent citing the impact of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

    Others pinned the rise on contract and order cancellation or delays, as well as weaker consumer confidence. Jo Robinson UK&I financial restructuring leader at EY said the warnings showed the “variety of structural changes and companies” firms are being forced to navigate.

    “This is not a conventional economic cycle… since the pandemic, supply-side disruption including material and labour shortages, energy shocks, tariffs and wider geopolitical disruption has become far more significant,” he said.

    “Companies are also facing existential questions about their business models, as consumer behaviour evolves and AI reshapes competitive positions and routes to market.”

    Nearly 20 per cent of UK listed businesses have issued a profit warning in the last twelve months.

    Housebuilders buckled

    The construction and household goods sectors were identified as the London-listed firms with the highest number of warnings during the period, totalling eight.

    This included six warnings from listed housebuilders, taking the total for the year to date to 14, surpassing the 10 issued by builders during the peak of the 2008 global financial crisis.

    Vistry, Persimmon and Taylor Wimpey were among the builders who released new warnings, citing cost inflation, lower sales rates and muted first-time buyer demand.

    Industrial support services, including Hays and Bunzl, as well as material firms also issued six profit warnings in the period.

    “Housebuilding has become the epicentre of these cost and interest rate pressures. The sector will be hoping that confirmation of the Government’s renewed support for first-time buyers will improve reservations and transaction volumes, although key details including eligibility, local price caps, developer contributions and timing are all still to be confirmed,” said Claire Gambles, financial restructuring strategy partner at EY.

    Policy change problems

    Robinson added the relentless “pace of policy change” is also making capital allocation harder for businesses, as forecasts and investments can quickly become inaccurate. 

    He said: “With the Autumn Budget around the corner, profit warnings linked to policy change and uncertainty, once concentrated around fiscal events or elections, have become a regular feature of our data.

    “In today’s fiscal and financing environment, where many earnings pressures are linked to external shocks or competitive and technological disruption, boards that act early instead of waiting for conditions to improve will retain more options.”

    The strange, freeing pursuit of bog swimming in wild Estonia

    I am a Princess Fiona seeking her Shrek. My best chance of finding my lonely yet loveable ogre and getting our long-overdue Happily Ever After, as every DreamWorks fan knows, is in a swamp. Hackney Marshes and Walthamstow Wetlands have thus far failed to deliver the requisite calibre of hero, so this summer I headed further afield.

    My swampy destination? Haraka Bog in Kõrvemaa, an appropriately wet landscape an hour outside Tallinn, a place where Estonia’s flag mirrors the white sky, blue water, and blackness of the soil.

    More on Estonia: ‘Massive opportunity’ for UK firms as digital services could save public 75,000 years

    The wilds of Estonia: choose your bog

    Estonia is famously flat. It is a country of coastal plains and open skies, which makes Kõrvemaa feel like a secret that the Earth has been keeping to itself. Protected forest, bogs and mires, eskers, valleys and still forest lakes – this is the landscape of fairytale where any kind of magic could happen. As we walked through the valleys and between the pine trees, my forest guide, Marilin Pehka, kept repeating: “Be silent. Nature is already telling you what you need to hear. You are already having a conversation with it.”

    Bogs are ecosystems where organic plant matter does not fully decompose but is deposited as peat. They are climate change fighting miracles, trapping carbon for 10,000 years or more. And although bogs and swamps might have a bad reputation for being dirty or smelly, nothing could be further from the truth: they are complex, well-balanced habitats, rare and beautiful wetlands where specialised plants and ground birds thrive.

    With an overcast sky, the water in Haraka Bog looked metallic and dark, with ripples circling out from the occasional plops or rain. I had clomped in blue plastic boots along the narrow boardwalk through the forest, listening to the wind shaking the trees and to the occasional twittering of the birds. And as I walked, I prepared mentally to strip everything off and surrender myself to nature. It wasn’t as if there were many spectators around.

    It was bracingly cold, but my heart rate quickened and my mind became enlivened, too. It felt as if it were not just clothes that I had shed. With all my layers off, I could completely let go, swimming in the middle of the bog, in light rain, completely naked. With bog swimming, it seems that Estonians understand how to fully experience nature, that if you approach the water, or the forest, naked, vulnerable, and in your most natural state, you can be reborn time and again and face the world anew.

    How to sauna in Estonia

    Uuejärv Nature Retreat is on a nature reserve which was previously a Soviet-era military training base. Its rustic sauna is heated by a wood-burning stove. During a guided sauna session you experience vihtlemine, the practice of beating one’s own body with bundled birch or oak leaves, which boosts circulation and is certainly invigorating.

    Where to stay

    Accommodation inside Kõrvemaa is sparse. I stayed in one of the Kuuse Concept Houses (kuusemajad.ee), set within dense spruce and pine forest near the Sportland Kõrvemaa Hiking and Ski Resort. The cabins are built in a Scandinavian style that does not so much sit in the forest as belong to it, with floor-to-ceiling glass walls that dissolve the boundary between inside and out. You wake up to trees. You fall asleep to trees. The only sounds are the ones the forest makes, the creak of branches and whatever is moving through the undergrowth outside.

    What to eat

    Chef Ellery Powell might be Norfolk-born and -bred, but he moved to Estonia more than a decade ago, and he pays tribute to his adopted homeland in each meal he cooks for guests staying at the Concept Houses. He sources every ingredient within a 50 km radius in Körvermaa, and, often, from much closer: I picked golden chanterelles (kukeseen) on my walk in the forest, and Ellery sauteed them in butter before me. He also treated me to salmon tartare, carefully wrapped under an umbrella of Estonian clover; and seabass with a white wine sauce, sprinkled in dill. 

    To understand a culture, you have to indulge in its cuisine. Food will mend the cracks whenever language is a barrier. And Ellery speaks ‘Estonian cuisine’ very well.

    The Prime Minister has flirted with the idea of letting football fans drink alcohol on terraces again and it could have an impact on how we measure fandom, writes Ben McMahon.

    Settle into your Wembley Stadium seat for today’s NFL game and you can roar on the Jaguars with a cool Coors in hand. Visit the Hill Dickinson Stadium in May for rugby league’s Magic Weekend and you can drink Guinness from a two-pint cup. Planning to visit those same stadiums on a England or Everton matchday, however? 

    You’ll do well to slip a Shloer into the stands. 

    As PM Andy Burnham flirts with lifting the ban on football fans drinking in view of the pitch, the contrast of alcohol’s position among sports offers a unique insight into fandom. Just as F1 drivers spray champagne, Wimbledon-goers sip Pimm’s and darts fans fling lager, every sport has its own rituals and unwritten rules. But what adds fizz to one fan experience can burst the bubble of another.

    Businesses operating around sport must drill down into the distinctions. Even if Burnham relaxes the ban, brands can’t just think, “Great, now what can we sell to football fans?”. The most important question, as always, remains: “What actually adds value to the experience people have come for?”

    Alcohol a fuel to the fire?

    Football clubs enjoy a level of fandom that other sports would give their right leg for. A deep-rooted sense of community, belonging and, in some cases, tattoos, guarantees fan loyalty even through the biggest defeats. The Premier League in particular is one of modern Britain’s greatest exports.

    But that tribalism has a darker side. In the 1970s and 80s, British football spilled into hooliganism and violence, with alcohol often adding fuel to the fire. 

    Since the ban was introduced in 1985, the sport’s culture has changed. More than 5,500 arrests were recorded at league matches in the 1984-85 season; today, football-related police action equates to just four incidents per 100,000 attendees, and even the recent highly charged “Dockers Derby” between Millwall and West Ham recorded just six arrests. 

    But has football moved far enough from its past behaviours to justify reintroducing the fuel that fed them? 

    Raising a glass to innovation

    Football’s tribalism hasn’t disappeared. It’s still what makes the sport so powerful. The Premier League hardly has a problem persuading people to turn up – but nor is its next generation of fans crying out for another place to buy a lager.

    Younger audiences are drinking differently, if at all. They’re also expecting more from live entertainment, like stronger fan interactivity and digital integration. Putting alcohol back into the stands sounds great for drinks companies, but is it a good argument for the modern football experience? 

    The 2022 World Cup in Qatar offered an interesting live experiment. The late decision to ban alcoholic beer sales from stadiums entirely made huge headlines at the time. However, on-site innovations, from fast-track entry gates to entertainment zones, still showed that a global football experience could appeal to fans across cultures without alcohol sitting at its centre.

    Think outside the box

    The debate offers a bigger opportunity to follow Fifa’s lead, look beyond the pint and ask what else could make the experience better.

    Other sports are already making huge strides here. Cricket has introduced entirely new short formats in T20 and The Hundred, while NBA jumbotrons run live fan-focused segments like kiss cams and dance-offs during in-game lulls. Football itself tested a new Super Bowl-style halftime show at the recent World Cup final, plus activations and in-stadium augmented reality tools. 

    The prime opportunity for businesses sits in that space around the sport. NFL-style tailgate parties, for example, could turn the hours before kick-off into somewhere fans meet, eat and spend time together – rather than a march from the pub to the stadium bar. It builds commercial value because it first creates something worthwhile for the audience.

    The same principle applies to every type of sport. At Goodwood’s motoring festival, eBay Garage tapped into the knowledge of the crowd. It worked because it added to what people had come to enjoy, rather than competing with it.

    Play the fandom occasion, not just the audience

    Sponsorship can buy access to an audience but the key is understanding what makes that audience tick.The real test is asking what fans are turning up for. 

    As this country’s national sport, top-flight football doesn’t have any issues attracting audiences. So any legislative decision that changes the fabric of the matchday experience must show a clear net benefit for the people watching it, rather than simply a commercial upside for the businesses selling into it.     This summer’s transfer window again showed the purchasing power of the Premier League, with almost £3.5bn being spent on transfer fees. And, while there were players being bought from foreign teams, there was also a significant number of very high value transfers between Premier League clubs this summer, which is notable compared to previous transfer windows.

    Given the Manchester City case, most people are now aware of the Premier League’s profit and sustainability rules (PSR), and it is clear that these have been relevant for recruitment at club level. However, could the abolition of the Remittance Basis in April 2025 have dissuaded overseas-based players from making the move to the UK?

    Old tax rules

    Previously, players at the top teams who played games in Europe could claim relief on those games under the Overseas Workday Relief (OWR) regime. As an example, if a player plays 10 per cent of their games overseas, then they could exempt 10 per cent of their salary from UK tax for the first three tax years (subject to certain conditions).

    They also had a period of up to 15 years where non-UK income and gains (outside of their salary) could be sheltered from UK tax under the Remittance Basis, as long as these were not brought to the UK.

    New regime

    However, the new Foreign Income and Gains (or FIG) regime has rung in important changes since being introduced from 6 April 2025.

    This regime provides a full exemption on non-UK income and gains, which is more generous than the Remittance Basis. However, the FIG regime is only available for four tax years which, given the way the transfer windows fall, would likely only last a player for three seasons.

    While the period that OWR can be claimed has been extended to four tax years (from three), this is limited to a total amount of £300,000 per year. This is a significant sum for most people, but for players at the top teams who are earning in excess of this amount a week, it severely weakens the appeal of this relief.

    Impact on players

    The impact of these new rules means that there is a potentially more generous regime available for those who would not benefit from OWR, however for a much shorter period.

    As such, for a player who may already have built significant wealth from their playing career, the FIG regime does not provide the mid-term tax benefits that the Remittance Basis afforded. For footballers, having consistency with their tax position is extremely important, especially as they only have a relatively short career to earn these levels of income.

    This surely is a consideration for non-UK players when considering offers from the Premier League compared to, say, renegotiating a deal at their existing club.

    Also, given that players who are currently playing in England are already caught by the UK tax system, is this a consideration for clubs looking to buy from other Premier League teams? 

    It is not a stretch to think that a newly recruited footballer from outside the UK will have an eye on the end of the FIG regime and be looking to move abroad after three seasons in the UK.

    At the same time, we have also seen a rise in British players moving abroad, including to countries with attractive tax regimes such as Saudi Arabia and Italy.

    While I don’t think there will be much public sympathy for highly paid footballers in the lead up to the Budget, could we see a relaxation of the recently introduced rules to keep the Premier League as the global force it has grown into, especially given the negative attention of the recent Manchester City case?

    Adam Jefferies is a director at PKF Littlejohn.

    Luxury house prize draw platform Omaze has appealed against HMRC over whether paid entries in its prize draws are subject to standard-rate VAT.

    An Omaze spokesperson told City AM the platform “has been paying VAT in the UK since 2021.”

    Omaze lists itself on its website as “not a charity raffle, house or cash raffle or house or cash lottery but a prize draw”.

    An organisation that offers a free entry route to a draw, such as a postcard option, avoids being regulated as a lottery under the Gambling Act, and HMRC categorises the service as a prize draw, meaning its paid entries do not qualify for the VAT exemption that regulated lotteries receive.

    However, earlier this year, Labour MP Dan Tomlinson, who was responsible for HMRC and tax policy until July, confirmed that prize draws offering both paid and free entry routes “are not eligible for VAT exemption and paid entries will be subject to VAT at the standard rate of 20 per cent.”

    Appeal ‘seeks clarity and consistency’ for industry

    Since launching in the UK in 2020, after being founded in the US in 2012, Omaze has run prize draws where entrants can win multi-million-pound houses, cars, or money for a relatively small fee.     The fundraising platform donates a proportion of the draw proceeds to a charity, and guarantees a minimum donation of £1m to its partner charities with each draw.

    “Our appeal seeks clarity and consistency in how VAT applies across the prize draw industry.     But Neville’s remarks could – with a bit of imagination – just as easily apply to the frenzied speculation in the run-up to this month’s Budget.

    Unlike his kite-flying, pitch-rolling predecessor, John Healey has remained notably tight-lipped on the composition of his maiden fiscal event.     But the one tax hike that has looked nailed on ever since the Rotherham MP named the date of his Budget – the “banker”, if you will – has been a windfall tax of one form or another on the City’s eminent banking sector.

Healey is still, says The Guardian, weighing his options. One move under consideration is to reverse Jeremy Hunt’s reduction of the bank surcharge.     It is – despite an intensive and relentless rearguard action from banking execs – a fate to which many in the sector were resigned. And – as the sector’s indefatigable industry bodies have warned – it will also eat into the price and volumes loans banks can afford to issue to capital-starved SMEs, choking off growth in the engine room of the UK economy.

      New inheritance tax rules will drastically alter how people use their pensions, and put a lot of individuals in difficult positions, writes Steve Gauke

      For years, pensions have been one of the most effective ways for families to pass wealth to the next generation. But from April 2027, that will change, with most unused pension funds being brought into the scope of inheritance tax.

      The problem isn’t simply that more families will face an inheritance tax bill. It’s that many may not realise they’re affected until it’s too late to prepare. We risk sleepwalking into a situation where thousands of families face unexpected tax liabilities at an already difficult time. Many families have planned around the old legislation, leaving a potential knowledge gap between the government distributing the new rules and the families who must understand them.

      The scale of the change is significant; the government’s estimates suggest that around 10,500 estates will pay inheritance tax for the first time in 2027 to 2028, and that a further 38,500 will pay more, with the average bill expected to rise by around £34,000. These are, of course, only estimates, but the changes will drastically alter how people use their pensions in response. This shift will put a lot of individuals in difficult positions, after all, behind every one of those figures is a family who will be asked to find a large sum of money at a very difficult time. When you consider the cost of living crisis, and how many families are asset rich but cash poor, changes like these will have a huge impact on people’s lives.

      The pension changes coming into effect in April 2027 may increase the inheritance tax payable by affected estates, potentially leaving beneficiaries with a larger tax bill and a smaller inheritance than anticipated. This adds to existing cash-flow pressures: beneficiaries can wait six to 12 months for their inheritance, while inheritance tax is generally due by the end of the sixth month after death. The changes won’t necessarily lengthen that wait, but executors usually need to pay the tax, or the first instalment where instalments are permitted, before obtaining probate. Under the new rules, beneficiaries may only be able to access around half of the affected pension benefits for up to 15 months. 

      This is the core of the problem. On paper families are inheriting a significant amount of wealth. But in practice, they have very little cash available to pay the bills in front of them. The good news is that families still have time to prepare. The first step is to have open conversations about inheritance; however uncomfortable they may feel. Understand what an estate is likely to include, locate important documents and establish whether the upcoming changes could create an inheritance tax liability.

      It’s also important to consider how any tax bill would actually be paid. Seeking independent financial advice, understanding the available payment arrangements and exploring options for accessing funds where necessary can help prevent difficult decisions being made under pressure. For example, a probate or inheritance loan, gives families early access to part of their inheritance, so that nobody is forced into a hurried sale.

      Families will plan around whatever the rules are, but what they need now from the government is clarity, enough time to prepare and some flexibility when the system moves more slowly than the bills arrive. Inheritance should not become an unnecessary financial burden simply because families were unaware of the rules or unable to access their money when they needed it most.

      Steve Gauke is managing director at Provira

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

]]> A telemarketer refused to keep his webcam on for nine hours a day while working from home and was fired the next day — a Dutch court ruled the demand invaded his privacy and ordered his employer to pay him roughly €75,000 https://siliconcanals.com/d-a-telemarketer-refused-to-keep-his-webcam-on-for-nine-hours-a-day-while-working-from-home-and-was-fired-the-next-day-a-dutch-court-ruled-the-demand-invaded-his-privacy-and-ordered-his-employ/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:15:27 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109737

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

Agility says Digit 5 is engineered for unfenced work near people; its runtime, charging and daily-productivity figures remain manufacturer specifications ahead of planned 2027 customer access.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: An earlier version miscounted the number of charge cycles in a 24-hour day and said early access was more than a year away. The idealised 90-to-9-minute ratio implies about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging; early access is planned for the first half of 2027.

Agility Robotics has unveiled Digit 5, the fifth generation of its bipedal warehouse robot, and the headline change is the safety cage — specifically, its absence. Earlier Digit models, like most industrial robots, operated inside fenced cells to keep people out of reach. Digit 5 is designed to work in the open, using sensors and a separate safety controller that can make it stop, back away or drop into a seated position when a person gets close, according to the company’s hardware rundown from The Robot Report.

The robot stands 5 feet 11 inches tall and weighs 284 pounds, roughly the mass of two adult humans packed into a torso, legs and a pair of articulated arms. That weight matters less as a curiosity than as context for what follows: a machine that heavy needs a battery system that can be recharged fast enough to stay useful across a full shift, and Agility has built its pitch to investors and warehouse customers around exactly that number.

The 90-minute run, nine-minute charge math

Digit 5 runs for about 90 minutes on a charge and returns to full power in roughly 9 minutes, a figure Agility frames as a 10-to-1 run-to-charge ratio, up from the 2-to-1 ratio it says the previous Digit 4 managed, per the company’s own announcement. In practical terms, that means a robot could in theory swap onto a charger for the length of a coffee break and be back on the floor before a human coworker finishes one.

The idealised arithmetic gives each 99-minute cycle 90 minutes of runtime and nine minutes of charging. Repeating that ratio across 24 hours yields about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging before allowing for maintenance, handoffs or faults. That is the basis for the company’s more conservative claim that Digit 5 can deliver more than 20 productive hours in a 24-hour day.

What a 20-hour day actually means

Agility is measuring two things and projecting a third. The 90-minute runtime and 9-minute recharge are specifications the company attaches to Digit 5’s battery hardware. The timing of the announcement lines up with a corporate transition. The company also plans to extend sales into the European Union and United Kingdom alongside its existing North American base, pending regulatory approval in those markets. Those dates put Digit 5’s actual commercial debut several months out from this week’s unveiling, and every performance figure attached to the robot right now, from its 90-minute runtime to its 20-hour workday, is a specification and a projection. Still, this has not yet been measured on a customer floor.

Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. An hour disappears into the phone and the honest inventory afterwards runs to three items: a man cutting marble, somebody’s strong opinion about interest rates, a dog on a skateboard.

None of it is retained in any way worth having. The hour still lands like work.

That mismatch, between the feeling of effort and the absence of anything learned, has a reasonable research explanation behind it, and willpower barely features in it.

A feed is a run of cold starts

Reading a book is one long continuous job. The brain loads a setting, a cast, an argument, and then keeps using that same setup for as long as the reading lasts.

A feed offers nothing of the kind.

Each post arrives with its own subject, tone, format and rules, which means the machinery of attention has to reconfigure itself before any of the content can be processed.

A feed adds another recurring job: a verdict. Each item has to be sized up for whether it is true, whether it is funny, whether it is aimed at anyone in particular. That call gets made before the thing can be dismissed, and then made again at the next one, and the one after that.

Psychologists have taken that reconfiguration apart. In a paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans described two stages: goal shifting, meaning the decision to do this now instead of that, and rule activation, meaning the swap of mental instructions from the old job to the new one. Both stages take time. A single switch might cost only a few tenths of a second. That sounds trivial until you count the switches inside an hour of scrolling.

Their experiments used arithmetic and shape-sorting rather than phones, so applying the finding to a feed is an inference, not a measurement.

The part that stays behind

Switching also leaves something on the floor. Sophie Leroy, now a professor at the University of Washington Bothell, coined the term attention residue in a 2009 paper in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, after experiments in which people were pulled off one task and pushed onto another. Performance on the second task dropped, because a slice of their attention was still parked on the first, and the effect was sharpest when the first task had been left unfinished.

Scrolling has the shape of that setup. Post after post is dropped mid-thought and replaced by the next one, which looks a great deal like the unfinished condition Leroy identified as the costly one. Her participants were working through lab tasks, though. The parallel to a phone is drawn by analogy, and nobody has run the experiment there.

Forty-seven seconds

Gloria Mark, a professor of informatics at the University of California, Irvine, has been logging how long people stay on a single screen since 2004. Back then the average was about two and a half minutes. In an interview with the University of California, she put the recent figure at roughly 47 seconds, with a median of 40, meaning half of all observed stretches were shorter than that.

That number needs handling with care. It is assembled from separate studies across two decades, not one group of people followed the whole way, and what it measures is screen behaviour. People still read long books. They just do it somewhere other than a browser tab.

Why a book behaves differently

Does the medium itself change how much gets understood? Pablo Delgado of the University of Valencia and three co-authors pooled 54 studies covering more than 171,000 participants in a meta-analysis for Educational Research Review, and found a consistent, modest advantage for paper. The gap widened when reading was timed instead of self-paced, held for informational texts but not narrative ones, and grew across the years studied, an unhelpful trend for anyone expecting digital natives to close it.

Pooling dozens of experiments makes that result sturdier than any single study, though the effect itself stays small.

Maryanne Wolf, who studies the reading brain at UCLA, argues in an op-ed for the Guardian that skimming squeezes out the slower processes that make reading useful: drawing inferences, making analogies, testing whether a claim is true, stepping into another person’s point of view. Move the eye fast enough and there is no room left for any of it.

Fatigue needs its own explanation, and it comes from a separate strand of Mark’s research.

In a study presented at the 2008 CHI conference, Mark, working with Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke, interrupted people mid-task and measured what happened. The interrupted group finished faster, with no drop in quality, which was the surprise. They also reported more stress, more frustration, more time pressure and more effort.

Compensation, in other words.

The brain appears to cover the cost of fragmentation by spending harder. Mark’s participants were working rather than scrolling, and the equivalent test has not been run on a feed, so the link is suggestive rather than established. Even so, the flatness and irritability at the end of a long scroll, the vague sense of having been mugged, match what those participants described.

Which puts the whole exercise in a different light. An hour on a feed involves several hundred small decisions made at speed, each one demanding a quick ruling on what the thing is and whether it matters. The content was the least of it. The deciding was the job.

Nobody sends an invoice for that. The tiredness is the receipt.

The rest played buyers, who could earn bonuses for accurately predicting how honest sellers would be.

In the first four studies, a seller counted as honest only if a reply named the defect. Staying quiet counted as dishonest, and so did a dodge like a battery that “isn’t brand new.”

The first pilot set the pattern. Of 76 online workers playing sellers, 63.2 percent picked a truthful opening message over one describing the iPod as being in excellent condition. Of 85 observers given the same information, 43.5 percent predicted the truthful one.

In Study 1, the 176 sellers wrote their own replies to “What can you tell me about it?” and “Anything else?” Of those sellers, 51.7 percent disclosed the battery problem, while the 270 buyers guessed, on average, that 43.2 percent would. With the scooter and a direct question in Study 2, three quarters of sellers disclosed the fault.

The rate swung with the setup. One cause, a direct question, got its own test; other swings the researchers could not fully explain. Until the last study, the exchanges were also largely scripted, with sellers answering pre-written buyer messages rather than a live counterpart.

The way the question is asked

Study 3, with 483 participants, gave half the sellers the pointed “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” and half the open “What can you tell me about them?” Buyers here were not told about the static, which is closer to how a real listing works.

The direct question made sellers more likely to mention the noise. Buyers’ predictions did not move with it.

The gap between expected and actual honesty was statistically significant under the direct question and not under the open one, so even inside this paper it did not show up everywhere. Of several possible reasons Study 1 still found a gap with open questions, the authors single out one: sellers there had two chances to come clean, and concealing twice may weigh more on a seller’s conscience than concealing once.

A few minutes of small talk

Study 5 was the only one that paired people live. It matched 422 participants into 211 buyer-seller pairs on an online platform, and some pairs first spent three minutes chatting about something they had enjoyed recently or how they unwind after a busy day.

Across the study, buyers rated their seller’s likely honesty at 6.56 on a ten-point scale, while coders scored the sellers’ actual replies at 7.51. Among pairs who chatted first, that difference was no longer statistically significant. Sellers’ scores did not differ significantly between the two conditions. The chat raised buyers’ expectations of honesty instead.

Study 4 tried a different nudge on 358 participants. Some buyers were asked about the seller’s moral concerns before predicting, others afterward. Thinking about the seller’s conscience first raised buyers’ expectations, and the gap was nearly halved.

It did not close. The authors suggest one reason: 85 percent of sellers in that study disclosed, a rate higher than in the matching condition of Study 3 for reasons they say are not readily apparent.

Where the suspicion comes from

Study 2 measured three motives, adding the pull of money to the two that Study 1 had tracked. The 214 management undergraduates who took part rated, on a seven-point scale, how much the seller had been weighing being decent, feeling guilty, and getting the best price. Sellers put their concern with being a decent person at 4.99, and buyers guessed 3.78. Buyers put the seller’s interest in money at 6.03; sellers reported 5.06.

The sellers still cared about the money. They cared about it less, and about their own decency more, than the buyers pictured.

The paper’s explanation leans on moral typecasting, the idea that people tend to see others as either doers or feelers, rarely both. A seller holds the object and the information, so, the authors argue, a buyer casts them as a doer, and the competitive setting makes that doer look like someone chasing an advantage rather than guarding a clean conscience. In the abstract’s words: “While sellers tended to be honest because of moral identity concerns, buyers expected them to be driven primarily by self-interest.”

Two duller explanations get a hearing too, and the authors say their own mechanism is not the only one. Poor forecasting in general, they point out, gives no reason to expect guesses to run low rather than high. Plain caution, a buyer bracing for the worst to avoid a loss, gets mixed treatment: the Study 4 discussion offers it as a possible added force, while the general discussion says it cannot explain the results, because in the first pilot observers with nothing at stake still underestimated the sellers.

Their mediation analyses deserve a lighter touch than the abstract’s sentence suggests. Buyers and sellers answered parallel versions of the motive questions rather than the same ones, and the authors say the results should be “cautiously interpreted” for that reason. Sellers rated their motives after choosing whether to disclose, which leaves room for a flattering story told afterward, though the authors argue buyers’ parallel ratings may reduce that concern. And in Study 1, the measure of anticipated guilt and related feelings showed no significant difference between buyers and sellers.

Small stakes, narrow scope

The stakes stayed small. Most bonuses were paid by lottery, and a seller in Study 1 had a five percent chance of earning at most $7. The authors grant that low stakes may keep self-interest from fully switching on, while citing earlier work that finds self-interest at work even when stakes are small.

The honesty studied was one kind: telling a buyer about a defect the seller knew. Misrepresenting a bottom price or inventing urgency, both named by the authors, were outside the design. They describe the findings as “based primarily on Western participant samples,” and the sales were one-off exchanges between strangers, chosen to keep reputation largely out of play. Ongoing work relationships and repeat customers sit outside what was measured.

Suspicion is sometimes the sensible response, and the paper says so. A buyer facing a salesperson expected to use persuasion tactics, or shopping where one side knows far more than the other, as with used cars, has good reason for care. The paper does not argue for trusting everyone. It asks for work on when doubting a counterpart’s honesty hurts a negotiator and when it protects one.

Every finding in this piece comes from the published text and tables of one paper, read by an editorial desk that reports on research and does not train negotiators; the supplementary files the paper points to could not be opened. The studies compared predictions with replies across hundreds of people, which says something about buyers and sellers like the ones studied, taken as groups, and cannot tell anyone whether the particular seller in their inbox is being straight with them. For a purchase that matters, sensible safeguards include an independent inspection, a written description of the item’s condition, and the buyer protection some platforms offer.

This paper did not measure what the gap costs. The authors’ illustration is a used car that looks too good to be true, and a buyer who distrusts the seller, walks away, and settles for something worse. Examining what the honesty gap does to the outcomes of negotiations is what they call an important next step; they also call for testing the idea where far more money is at stake.

]]> Quote of the day: “Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself” https://siliconcanals.com/d-quote-of-the-day-sometimes-you-find-yourself-in-the-middle-of-nowhere-and-sometimes-in-the-middle-of-nowhere-you-find-yourself/ Thu, 17 Sep 2026 10:45:39 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109380

What happens when your plans collapse, your phone dies, and you're stranded at a gas station thousands of miles from home—and it's the best thing that could've happened.]]>

The last time I was properly lost, I was standing at a petrol station somewhere north of Chiang Rai with a dead phone, a warm bottle of water and a dog who clearly ran the place. My bus had left without me. I had four hours to wait, nothing to do and no way to tell anyone about it.

It was the calmest I had been in about eighteen months.

Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself.

Yes, it is the sort of line that ends up engraved on a bracelet and screwed to somebody’s kitchen wall. Both of which have happened, it turns out. I went looking for whoever wrote it and found nothing, only evidence that it has been circulating since at least 2014 with no author attached. Anonymous, then. It holds up better than most things sold at a craft market.

Nowhere is mostly an absence of audience

Here is what I think the line is really about. Nowhere has very little to do with distance. It is any situation where nobody knows your job title.

In a city you are surrounded by people who already have a version of you loaded. The neighbour who thinks you are the loud one. The old colleague who still introduces you by the thing you did in 2019. You end up performing that version without noticing, because it is easier than correcting everybody.

Take the audience away and something odd happens. For a day or two you feel faintly useless, because nobody needs anything from you. Then the noise drops. You start hearing your own opinions, which are less impressive and a good deal more honest than the ones you say out loud.

That is the whole mechanism. No mysticism required.

The year my diary went blank

I lost my business, restaurants, during the pandemic. The deal was agreed over a phone call while I sat on a plastic chair in a dining room with the lights off, and it was the least bad option available to me at the time.

For years my day had been decided for me by suppliers, staff rotas and the seven o’clock rush. Then it was not. I woke up on a Tuesday with an empty calendar and genuinely no idea what a Tuesday was for.

I would love to tell you this was peaceful. I reorganised the same cupboard twice. I developed strong opinions about a neighbour’s parking. I rang people I had not spoken to in five years and could hear them wondering what I wanted.

The useful part arrived about three months in, once I had run out of things to tidy. With no restaurant to point at, I had to work out what I would actually do with a day if nobody was paying me for it. The answer was writing, which was inconvenient, as it pays considerably worse than a burger.

You can get lost for the price of a bus ticket

You do not need to sell a business or fly to Patagonia. Nowhere comes in small doses and most of them are free.

Pick a district of your own city you have no reason to visit and spend three hours there on foot. Not a famous one. A dull one, with hardware shops and a wet market and nothing on sale to anyone carrying a suitcase. I do this in Bangkok about once a month and I have never regretted it, though I have frequently regretted the shoes.

Go somewhere your phone cannot help you. Not switched off, just outgunned: the lanes are not on the map and the only language on offer is one you do not speak.

Be a beginner at something in public. Take a class where you are visibly the worst person in the room. It is physically uncomfortable for about twenty minutes. After that it stops mattering, and what is left is quite close to fun.

And if you do travel, leave one day entirely unplanned. No booking, no list, no reservation you have to walk fast to reach. Most people schedule a trip so tightly that they never get further than a warmer version of their normal week.

What actually turns up

Let me manage expectations. You do not come back from a petrol station with a revelation.

What you come back with is a shorter list. Two or three things you thought you cared about turn out to belong to somebody else. One or two things you have never mentioned to anyone are suddenly all you think about when there is nothing else to think about. That is it. It looks like very little on paper. It does not feel that way at thirty-eight, when you are still doing a job you picked at twenty-two to impress someone who stopped watching years ago.

There is a trap in this, though. Some people use the middle of nowhere as somewhere to hide, and the giveaway is that they keep having to go back. If every trip is an escape from the same unaddressed thing at home, the scenery is doing the work of a conversation you have been avoiding. Distance is excellent for seeing a problem clearly. It has never once solved one for me.

The dog at the petrol station, for the record, took no interest in any of this. He sat under the ice cabinet, moved twice in four hours, and had evidently worked something out about Wednesdays that I am still catching up on.

They’re often people whose sense of dignity was undermined so regularly that protecting it became something close to a full-time occupation https://siliconcanals.com/d-psychology-suggests-people-who-appear-offended-by-everything-arent-usually-seeking-drama-theyre-often-people-whose-sense-of-dignity-was-undermined-so-regularly-that-protecting-it-became-something-c/ Thu, 17 Sep 2026 10:45:02 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109377

Chronic offense-taking isn't performative outrage—it's a trauma response masquerading as oversensitivity.]]>

I used to think of a certain kind of person as a weather system. You know the type. You ask how the traffic was and somehow you have insulted their driving, their neighbourhood and their late mother. Everything lands as a slight. Everything requires a correction.

For years my take on this was simple and a bit smug. Attention seekers. People who enjoy the theatre of being wronged.

Then I started reading the actual psychology, and it turns out I had the story backwards. The people who seem offended by everything are rarely shopping for a fight. Most of them are running a security detail, and they have been running it since they were small.

When insults were the weather, everything looks like an insult

Here is the mechanism. If you grow up somewhere that regularly treats you as a target, your brain gets very good at spotting incoming fire. That is not a flaw. In the original environment it was survival. The problem is that the skill does not switch off when you move somewhere safer.

Psychologists call this hostile attribution bias, and it shows up early. Researchers followed around 1,300 children across nine countries and gave them scenarios where someone’s behaviour could be read as an accident or as deliberate. A shove in a corridor. A joke that could go either way. The children who consistently read hostile intent went on to show higher rates of persistent aggressive behaviour, even after accounting for how aggressive they had already been.

Two children see the same shove. One files it under accident, one files it under attack. Twenty years later, one of them is the adult who somehow takes offence at the weather report.

Being told you are too much is its own training

The other route in is quieter and I suspect more common.

Some people are not knocked around. They are simply corrected, constantly, about their own inner life. You are not upset. You are not tired. That did not hurt. Stop being dramatic. Clinicians call this an invalidating environment, a setting that consistently dismisses or punishes someone for expressing what they feel or need.

The theory behind that term was built to explain a specific clinical picture, so I would not go throwing it at your touchy colleague as a diagnosis. But the underlying logic travels. If your read on your own experience gets overruled a thousand times, you learn something ugly. You learn that your sense of things will not be taken seriously unless you make it loud.

And making it loud is exactly what the rest of us punish. We call it oversensitivity. We are reading the receipt and ignoring the purchase.

The tax the sensitive person pays

None of this is a free pass, and here is where it stops being sympathetic.

Researchers describe a disposition they call rejection sensitivity, meaning a tendency to anxiously expect rejection, spot it readily, and react hard when you think you have found it. People high in it tend to be less satisfied in their close relationships, and their partners report the same.

The trap is that the vigilance manufactures the thing it fears. You brace for the cold shoulder, so you go cold first. Your partner feels the chill and pulls back. Now you have evidence. Now the system that was built to protect your dignity has quietly started demolishing it.

I have watched this happen up close, over what I promise you was a genuinely neutral text message. There was no villain in that story. There was a very old alarm and a very ordinary Tuesday.

What actually helps when you are on the receiving end

Arguing about whether the offence was reasonable is a losing game. The alarm is not calibrated to this conversation. It was calibrated years ago, by somebody else.

Try naming the feeling without conceding the facts. Something like: I can see that landed badly, and I did not mean it that way. That costs you nothing on the question of intent, and it grants them something rare, which is agreement that their reaction was real. It does more work than an hour of you proving your innocence.

Be boringly consistent. Vigilance responds to evidence, not reassurance, and that takes months. You cannot talk someone out of a threat detector. You can only give it a long run of days where nothing bad happens.

And hold your line anyway. Understanding why someone snaps is not the same as accepting being snapped at. You can say plainly that you will not be shouted at and still mean everything above.

And if the thin skin is yours

Then start somewhere other than whether you were right. You often are. Slights are real, and some of the people telling you to calm down are exactly the ones worth watching.

The more useful question is what the alertness is costing you. Running security is expensive. It eats your Sundays. It makes you rehearse conversations that never happen and re-read messages for tone that was never there. My grandmother had a version of this. It made her formidable company. I think it also made her lonely.

So build a delay. When something lands wrong, wait a day before you respond. Graciousness has nothing to do with it. You are checking whether the feeling survives a night’s sleep. Usually it does not. The ones that do are worth taking seriously, and now you can take them seriously without the static.
